3	# The implicit bound of a static type parameter: what the team left, and what the curator was told
4	
5	Scout report, tree at `5da8144e4` (branch `main`), 2026-10-26. Retrieval only. Nothing here is a recommendation.
6	
7	## 0. How to read this report
8	
9	- **The three layers.** Section 1 is the language (what the team's texts say the bound is). Section 2 is the team's implementation on the JVM (the switch, its history, what the code and tests do with a bound, how the run time represents `Any`, tuples, arrows and `()`). Section 3 is Java interoperability. Section 4 is the revival's record and the transcripts. Section 5 lists what I could not find.
10	- **Parentless snapshots.** Many of the team's 2011-2012 commits in this repository are parentless full-tree snapshots (`research/authorship.md`, header; `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/records.md`, "The repository's history"). `git blame` on the current lines of `Shell.java`, `PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.java`, `NamingCzar.java`, `InstantiatingClassloader.java` and the Scala checker lands on `5a68404fd` (David Chase, 2012-07-19, "Added odd random longs to MagicNumbers", a root commit with no parent) or, for the classloader, on the revival's ASM upgrade `2f1fdbf2e` (blame with `-w --ignore-rev 2f1fdbf2e2` lands on `5a68404fd` again). So a blame hit is not where a line was written. I dated lines two ways:
11	  1. By content: the earliest commit, by commit time, whose version of the file contains the string (a small shell loop, "first appearance" below). This gives the commit that first holds a line, which is the author's commit or a later snapshot of it.
12	  2. By tree-to-tree diff against the snapshot's likely predecessor. For `91e71e62e` (Guy Steele, 2012-05-28) the predecessor is Steele's own previous commit `61f60e5fe`: `git diff --stat 61f60e5fe 91e71e62e -- . ':!Documentation'` gives 20 files, all on the subject (section 2.3). For `afb02f41d` (Steele, 2012-05-30) the predecessor is `d3f49be2f`: 9 files. The earlier record note `explorations/reviews/fill-overloads-ways.md:477-479` says these two diffs "cannot be isolated"; these two comparisons isolate them.
13	- **Dates.** Team commits are quoted with their git date and offset (`-0400` in 2012). Transcript entries are UTC.
14	- **Revival lines.** Where a cited line was written by the revival (author `Claude`, 2026), I say so. The switch lines themselves (`Shell.java:276-278`, `:324-326`, `:371-386`, `:1282`; `PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.java:132-144`, `:194-208`) are unchanged since the team's last commit: `git diff --stat 5a68404fd a874948ac -- <both files>` is empty, and `git log a874948ac..HEAD -G'ExtendsObjectPreDesugaring|extendsObject_pre_desugar' -- ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java` is empty.

88	- `Shell.java:403-404` (`compile`), `:410-411` (`link`), `:415-416` (`build`): `useCompilerLibraries()`; `:420-421` (`walk`): `useInterpreterLibraries()`.
89	- `PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.java:194-208` `forStaticParam`: with the switch off it calls `super`; with it on it rewrites the parameter through `rewriteStaticParamExtendsClause` (`:132-144`), which returns the clause unchanged if non-empty and otherwise `{Object}` built from `WellKnownNames.objectTypeName`. The header comment (`:37-44`), the `namesOnlyAny` and `namesOnlyAnyOrIndex` helpers (`:76-100`) and `isLibraryIndex` (`:127`) were edited or added by the revival (`4190069c4`, `153887360`); the static-parameter code (`:132-144`, `:194-208`) was not.

178	### 2.5 How the compiled run time represents `Any`, `Object`, tuples, arrows and `()`
179	
180	- **`Any`** is the JVM interface `fortress/AnyType$Any`: `TypeMapping.tex:87-89` ("the root of the Fortress type hierarchy and supertype of Tuples, Arrows, and Object"; first in `4a839480f`, David Chase, 2012-05-21); `NamingCzar.java:138-140`, `:225`; `runtimeSystem/Naming.java:137` (`ANY_TYPE_CLASS`), `:143` (`RTTI_GETTER_CLASS = ANY_TYPE_CLASS`). The Fortress source is `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fsi:14` `trait Any end` (first in `f5e78afde`, jmaessen, 2008-04-15). Every runtime value class extends `FValue`, `public abstract class FValue implements fortress.AnyType.Any` (`compiler/runtimeValues/FValue.java:14`), which declares `getRTTI()`. The class loader's generated `isA` methods test `instanceof fortress/AnyType$Any` and call `getRTTI` through it (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:1286-1330`).
181	- **`Object`** is a separate trait, `trait Object extends Any` (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:17`, `CompilerBuiltin.fss:354`, first in `c8d301411`, jmaessen, 2008-12-19; interpreter side `FortressBuiltin.fsi:32`, `2e3e67f18`). It declares the getters `asString`, `asExprString`, `asDebugString` (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:18-20`; `CompilerBuiltin.fss:355-357`); `Any` has no member (`AnyType.fsi:14`). It compiles to the interface `fortress/CompilerBuiltin$Object` (`TypeMapping.tex:84-85`: "the root for the Fortress trait hierarchy"). It is not `java/lang/Object`: `NamingCzar.java:170` `internalObject` is `Type.getInternalName(Object.class)`, used as the superclass of generated types (`CodeGen.java:5085-5087`).
182	- **Tuples**: interface `Tuple[\T1..Tn\]` with a super-interface `AnyTuple[\N\]` that extends `AnyType$Any`; the classes are generated by the loader (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:1676-1690`, `:2046-2074`; `TypeMapping.tex:141-154`, `:207-210`). Elements are read as `Any` (`FortressEncodings.tex:301-309` at `5c13fce7e`, dr2chase, 2011-01-29: `o1`..`oN` "returning `Fortress$AnyType$Any`"). `TupleRTTI.runtimeSupertypeOf` (`TupleRTTI.java:28-41`) is the Java test or an element-wise test of the same arity. `TypeMapping.tex:154`: tuple subtype queries "are compiled into element-by-element subtype queries". `:151` states the covariance with `Object` as the element top ("if X, Y, and Z each extend Object, then (X,Y,Z) extends (Object,Y,Z), ..."), and `:196` speaks of the subtyping between `(T,U,V)` and `(Object, Object, Object)` that "might be compiled ahead of time".
183	- **Arrows**: interface `Arrow[\dom..., range\]` with up to three `apply` methods (`TypeMapping.tex:156-167`; `InstantiatingClassloader.java:942-1000`, `:1185-1260`). `ArrowRTTI.runtimeSupertypeOf` (`ArrowRTTI.java:43-57`) is contravariant in inputs and covariant in the output. `TypeMapping.tex:167`: the third `apply` "receives the argument list as a single Tuple of the appropriate element types; this is necessary to support certain forms of generic instantiation (if a type parameter is instantiated with a Tuple, for example)".
184	- **`()`**: the value is `FVoid` (`compiler/runtimeValues/FVoid.java:14`, `extends FValue`, so it implements `AnyType.Any`); its RTTI is `VoidRTTI`, whose `runtimeSupertypeOf` answers true only for another `VoidRTTI` (`VoidRTTI.java:13-16`; "Fixed glitch with RTTI of void", David Chase, `a9c625b1e`, 2012-06-19); in generated names it is the snowman `☃` (`Naming.java:175`, `:305`; `TypeMapping.tex:107`, "`()` as a static parameter").
185	- **`Bottom`** is erased to `java/lang/Object` (`NamingCzar.java:206`, `81d727ad8`, David Chase, 2012-06-18, "Some cleanup related to bottom types name conversion and modeling in the JVM"; `:1297-1306`).
186	- **Generic classes** are template classes instantiated by the loader with RTTI objects as static arguments (`TypeMapping.tex:114-125`, `MethodMapping.tex:98-120`); `NamingCzar.forVarType` leaves a naked type variable as its name (`NamingCzar.java:1427-1431`), which the loader replaces at instantiation. The team's notes on the cost: `MethodMapping.tex:435`, "Covariant generics with Any-bounded static parameters (for example AnyList[\ T extends Any \]) will create special headaches because Tuple and Arrow type relationions are far too large to encode into the Java type system. One possibility will simply be to forbid that case; otherwise, it can be implemented by wrapping values ..." (the same sentence is in `FortressEncodings.tex` since `5c13fce7e`, 2011-01-29). `MethodMapping.tex:430`: "Each Fortress Object (perhaps not Any, meaning not Tuples, not Arrows) will have a method getRTTI()" (first in `c45132992`, David Chase, 2011-03-29).

<!-- A probe of what the compiled path (checker, code generator, class loader, run time) does with a tuple, an arrow and () as a static argument under the compile command's bound Object and under the bound Any, with the CompilerSystem tests and the compiled test tracks run under the bound Any. -->

# The bound `Any` on the compiled path: tuple, arrow and `()` static arguments

Base: `e0ec620a9` (code equal to `main`), worktree `/home/user/fortress-boundany` seeded from `/home/user/fortress-base23`, now removed. Machine: `nproc` 4, Intel Xeon @ 2.10 GHz, OpenJDK 25.0.4.1; the shape programs ran at `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, the JUnit runs at 4.

## The answer in short

- **Under the bound `Any`, the compiled path handles tuple and arrow static arguments.** Generic functions, generic objects, generic traits, dispatch to a generic arm, and `typecase` all compile, load and run in every shape, with a written argument and an inferred one. They behave exactly as the same programs with `extends Any` written do today: the class loader makes the same classes by name, and the program jars are the same under `javap -p -c -s`.
- **`()` as a static argument fails at run time under both settings** with `AbstractMethodError`, whenever a parameter has the type variable's type. This is row 339, and it does not depend on the bound.
- **Probing found a new defect that does not depend on the bound.** A generic dotted method whose single parameter has a tuple type dies at the call with `ClassCastException`. The tuple type can be written, as `(U, U)`, or come from a tuple static argument.
- **The checker's refusals under the bound `Object` are row 412.** Some programs pass the checker under that bound, and they are rows 470 and 691. In particular, `q = id((3, 4))` compiles under the compile command as it is, and silently runs `id(3)`.
- **The 23 `.test` files that cover the importers of `CompilerSystem` pass under both settings.** They give `OK (138 tests)` each time, with the same verdict lines.
- **The whole compiled tracks under the bound `Any`:**
  - compiler track: 1315 tests, 12 failures, in 10 tests;
  - library track: 86 tests, 0 failures;
  - othercompiler track: 263 tests, 0 failures.
- **Every one of the 10 red tests is a test-side cost, not a code defect.** One is the expected promotion, three are pinned diagnostics that print the bound, four wrote `where [\E extends Object\]` as a workaround, one test's premise rests on the bound `Object`, and one hits the compiler prelude's `||` at `Object`.

## Setting (ii): the smallest way to turn the pre-desugaring off

`fortress compile`, `link` and `build` call `Shell.useCompilerLibraries()` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java:404-449`). Its first line, `setExtendsObjectPreDesugaring(true)` (`Shell.java:372`), sets the switch. `PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.forStaticParam` reads that switch (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/desugarer/PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.java:195-208`). It is the only reader (grep for `ExtendsObjectPreDesugaring`). With the switch off, a static parameter with an empty `extends` clause keeps it empty. Its bound is then `Any`.

The rewriting of trait, object and object-expression `extends` clauses to `Object` is not under the switch (`:107-129`, called at `:163-190`). So under both settings every declared trait and object still extends `Object`. Only tuples, arrows and `()` lie outside `Object`.

The smallest change is that one line, set to `false`. For the probe I made it a property that defaults to `true` (the patch is at the end). That way both settings ran on one build:

- setting (i): the variable is unset, and the code path is that of `main`;
- setting (ii): `FORTRESS_PROBE_BOUND_OBJECT=false`.

The two settings also used different caches folders:

- **Setting (ii)'s caches.** Setting (ii) compiles the compiler's library under it too: I ran the library order into a private caches folder with the variable set. All five compiles exited 0, in 7, 23, 11, 2 and 2 s.
- **Setting (i)'s caches.**
  - The first 36 shape programs ran on the seeded build before the patch, against a copy of the seeded caches.
  - The later programs ran on the patched build with the variable unset, against a library order run on that build.
  - The two setting-(i) `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar` files are byte-identical: 0 of 246 entries differ.

Proof that the variable reached each JVM:

- `XXXImplicitBoundAny` compiles and runs under (ii): `kind of a Seal at Any ->  Seal at Any`. Under (i) it is refused: `The static argument Any does not satisfy the corresponding bound Object.`
- In the JUnit runs, that test turns red under (ii), with `Saw wrong failure. compile`.

## The shapes by setting

Each shape was written twice: U has no `extends` clause, and A has `extends Any` written, as a control. W writes the static argument and I leaves it to inference. "AME" stands for `AbstractMethodError`, "CCE" for `ClassCastException`, and "refused" for a checker error. Every program that compiled also loaded its classes; a failure is named where it happened.

Row 691's drop under (i), shown by one more program:

    id[\T\](x: T): T = x
    run(): () = do  q = id((3, 4)); r: ZZ32 = q + 1; println("q + 1 = " r)  end

- Under (i), the compile command as it is, it compiles and prints `q + 1 =  4`. The run method's bytecode pushes `iconst_3` alone and calls the closure `id⟦fortress|CompilerBuiltin%IntLiteral⟧`, so the `4` is dropped.
- Under (ii) it is refused: '(ZZ32, ZZ32)->ZZ32 is not applicable to an argument of type ((IntLiteral, IntLiteral), IntLiteral).'

The bound `Object` makes the pair unbindable to `T`. The checker then reads the pair as two arguments to a one-parameter generic and drops the second, as row 691 records for `g(a, a, a, a)`.

## What the class loader makes

I took these from each run's expanded classes (`-Dfortress.bytecodes.expanded.directory`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:83`) and read them with `javap -p -s -c`. Below, `FZZ32` stands for `com|sun|fortress|compiler|runtimeValues|FZZ32`.

- **The template carries no bound.** `Box⟦⟧` is compiled with `LT;` in its field and method descriptors. Its translation data holds the kind and the name only: `... object 1 4 type 1 T 0`. The U and A jars are the same under `javap`, and so are the setting-(i) and setting-(ii) jars of one program.
- **`Box` at a pair** gives two classes:
  - `BoxPairWU$\=Box⟦Tuple⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧⟧`, made from the static type. Its field is `L\=Tuple⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧;`. It has two constructors, `(L\=Tuple⟦…⟧;)V` and `(LFZZ32;LFZZ32;)V`.
  - Its twin `Box⟦ConcreteTuple⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧⟧`, made from the RTTI. `RTHelpers.getRTTIclass` names the class from each argument RTTI's `className()` (`runtimeSystem/RTHelpers.java:18-43`). A tuple RTTI calls itself `ConcreteTuple⟦…⟧` (`compiler/runtimeValues/TupleRTTI.java:43-49`).
  - Both classes take one interned RTTI, `Box$RTTIc.factory(Tuple*2$RTTIc.factory(FZZ32, FZZ32))`, so `typecase` works.
- **`Box` at an arrow** gives `Box⟦Arrow⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧⟧`, with the field `L\=Arrow⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧;`, and the twin `Box⟦AbstractArrow⟦…⟧⟧` (`ArrowRTTI.java:60-66`).
- **`id` at a pair** gives the closure `IdPairWU⚙$\=id⟦Tuple⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧⟧✉$✚Arrow⟦T,T⟧ extends \=AbstractArrow⟦Tuple⟦…⟧,Tuple⟦…⟧⟧`. It has `apply(L\=Tuple⟦…⟧;)L\=Tuple⟦…⟧;` and a spread `apply(LFZZ32;LFZZ32;)…`, because the arrow class reads a tuple domain as that many parameters.
- **`id` at an arrow** gives the closure `id⟦Arrow⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧⟧`, whose method is `apply(L\=Arrow⟦…⟧;)L\=Arrow⟦…⟧;`.
- **The trait** gives `TraitPairU$\=Holder⟦Tuple⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧⟧`, `Holder⟦Arrow⟦…⟧⟧` and `Holder⟦☃⟧`, each with its `$DefaultTraitMethods`.
- **`()`** gives `Box⟦☃⟧` and `IdUnitWA⚙$id⟦☃⟧✉$✚Arrow⟦T,T⟧ extends AbstractArrow⟦☃,☃⟧`. That closure defines `apply(Lcom/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FVoid;)LFVoid;`. The interface `Arrow⟦☃,☃⟧` declares `apply()LFVoid;`. Hence the AME of row 339.
- **The class lists are equal across the settings.** For each of 14 shape pairs, the A program under (i) and the U program under (ii) make the same classes by name, 6 to 32 each.

## The CompilerSystem tests, and the compiled tracks, under (ii) against (i)

27 components of `compiler_tests/` import `CompilerSystem`, and one more in `other_compiler_tests/` (grep `import CompilerSystem`; `library_tests/` has none). 25 of them have `.test` files: 23 files, with `Compiled7.test`, `Compiled90.test` and `AfterTypeChecking.test` covering several components each.

content.content:
27 components of `compiler_tests/` import `CompilerSystem`, and one more in `other_compiler_tests/` (grep `import CompilerSystem`; `library_tests/` has none). 25 of them have `.test` files: 23 files, with `Compiled7.test`, `Compiled90.test` and `AfterTypeChecking.test` covering several components each.

I ran them as one call of `ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> ProjectFortress/compiler_tests Compiled2.test XXX2h.test … AfterTypeChecking.test`, once per setting:

    (ii)  OK (138 tests)
    (i)   OK (138 tests)

Every verdict line is the same. The whole outputs differ only in timings and in the order of one line of `Compiled7`'s output at four threads. The three importers without a `.test` file give the same result under both settings when compiled directly:

- `Compiled220` runs and prints `3`;
- `Compiled250` is refused, 'Invalid overloading of f';
- `Compiled2PreTest3` dies on `args[0]` with no arguments.

The larger measurement was `ant testQuick` with `FORTRESS_PROBE_BOUND_OBJECT=false`. Ant's `junit` forks inherit the variable, and the red `XXXImplicitBoundAny` shows that they did:

    library        Tests run: 86, Failures: 0
    othercompiler  Tests run: 263, Failures: 0
    compiler       Tests run: 1315, Failures: 12, Errors: 0     BUILD FAILED

The counts equal the last gate's (`explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-22/gate/summary.txt`, 1315/86/263, all 0). That gate ran on code equal to the base's. The same 10 tests (12 JUnit failures) fail again under (ii) through `junit.sh`, and pass under (i) on the same build: `OK (12 tests)`. They fall into five groups:

| test | under (ii) | kind |
|---|---|---|
| `XXXImplicitBoundAny` | compiles: 'Saw wrong failure' | the promotion that row 412's fix owes |
| `XXX6bu`, `XXX6bv` (`Compiled6.bu`, `.bv`) | the same refusal, now printed `[\T\](T, T)->T` where `compile_err_equals` pins `[\T extends Object\]` | pinned text |
| `XXXInferCallArgumentControls` | the same 4 errors; the fourth now reads `BoxT[\Any\]` where the regex pins `BoxT[\Object\]` (the result-only parameter takes its bound, P-48) | pinned text |
| `OpenTypeChecker`, `ComprisesWhereFunctionalMethodChecker`, `ComprisesWhereOverrideChecker`, `XXXComprisesWhereFunctionalMethodBounds` | 'Invalid comprises clause: AnyBox has a comprises clause but its immediate subtype Box is not eligible to extend it.' | see below |
| `XXXOverrideGenericReturnTypeNotSubtype` | 1 error where it pins 2 | see below |
| `CoercionGenericFnCompiledRungC` (compile, link, run) | '(String, Object)->String is not applicable to an argument of type (String, T).' | see below |

The last three groups:

- **The four `comprises` tests** list `Box[\E\]` with `where [\E extends Object\]`, while `Box`'s own `E` is unbounded. Under (i), the pre-desugaring makes the two agree. Under (ii), `Box[\E\]` at an `E` outside `Object` is not covered.
  - Written `where [\E\]`, as the one library writes `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`, `OpenTypeChecker` passes the checker under (ii). Its compile then stops at the code generator's refusal of the trait's `where` clause (row 701), which is a typecheck test's normal end.
  - Under (i), that form is refused: 'The static argument E does not satisfy the corresponding bound Object.' So the tests wrote `Object` as a workaround for row 412.
- **`XXXOverrideGenericReturnTypeNotSubtype`** has `override f(x: Any): ZZ32` beside the inherited `f[\T\](x: T): T`.
  - Under (i), `T`'s domain is `Object`, which is strictly narrower than `Any`. So the declaration overrides, and its return type is refused.
  - Under (ii), the two domains are equal, so nothing is overridden. The rule then wants a refusal of an `override` that overrides nothing, which the checker never gives (row 653).
  - The test's premise rests on the bound `Object`.
- **`CoercionGenericFnCompiledRungC`'s** `"…" || y` has `y: T` unbounded. The compiler prelude's String `||` takes `Object` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:38`). The one library has `opr ||(a:String, b:Any)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2528`). This is a prelude limit that lasts until the switch-over.

Library jars under (ii) against (i), on the same build:

- `AnyType`, `CompilerBuiltin` (278 entries), `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are byte-identical.
- 6 of `CompilerLibrary`'s 246 entries differ: `FilteredRange`, `GeneratorZZ32$DefaultTraitMethods`, `SeqGenZZ32`, `SeqGeneratorZZ32$DefaultTraitMethods`, `CompilerLibrary.class` and `Just`'s `nest` closure.
  - The dispatch tests the `ReductionString` and `ReductionZZ32` arms of `generate`, `seqgenerate` and `__generate` in the other order.
  - In `nest`, the run-time inference code orders the operands of `runtimeSupertypeOf` differently and keeps another RTTI. That code reads the bound (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java:1500-1524`).
- Each setting is deterministic: two library orders under (ii) gave the same bytes, and so did (i) seeded and rebuilt.
- No test showed the difference.

## What the code shows for each failure, and its row

- **`()` (row 339).** The template's `apply(LT;)` becomes `apply(LFVoid;)`. The arrow interface instantiated at `Arrow⟦☃,R⟧` reads the slot `☃` as an empty domain. That is the void cases at `InstantiatingClassloader.java:604-605`, `:1009-1010`, `:1116` and `:1229`.
  - `NamingCzar` writes `☃` both for a parameterless arrow (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/NamingCzar.java:1155-1170`) and for the tuple type `()` (`:1259-1260`). So one parameter of type `()` and no parameter share one spelling.
  - For a tuple domain, the class loader adds the spread `apply`. For `()`, it adds no nullary bridge.
  - The `javap` above confirms the row's "unverified reading". This is independent of the bound: A under (i) fails alike.
- **A generic dotted method with a single tuple-typed parameter: new, no row.**
  - `CodeGen.receiverPrependedDomainType` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:6250-6263`) builds the domain of the closure that the call casts to. Where the method's domain is a tuple type, it prepends the receiver to the tuple's elements. It cannot tell a single parameter of tuple type from several parameters. The team's comment there reads: 'I think we start to have a problem here in the future, when generics can be parametrized by tuples.'
  - So `b.wrap[\(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]((2, 3))` casts to the three-place `AbstractArrow⟦Tuple⟦Box⟦FZZ32⟧,FZZ32,FZZ32⟧,…⟧` (`emitFindGenericMethodClosure`, `:6316-6355`) and calls a three-argument `apply`.
  - The class loader makes the closure from the template `Arrow⟦Tuple⟦☝,U⟧,Box⟦U⟧⟧`, at `U := Tuple⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧`. That is a two-place arrow whose second place is a pair.
  - First stack lines:

        java.lang.ClassCastException: class MethPairWU⚙$\=Box☝wrap⟦…⟧✉$\=✚Arrow⟦Tuple⟦☝,U⟧,MethPairWU%Box⟦U⟧⟧ cannot be cast to class \=Arrow⟦Tuple⟦java|lang|Object,java|lang|Object,java|lang|Object⟧,java|lang|Object⟧
          at \=AbstractArrow⟦Tuple⟦MethPairWU%Box⟦FZZ32⟧,FZZ32,FZZ32⟧,MethPairWU%Box⟦Tuple⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧⟧⟧.castTo(Unknown Source)
          at MethPairWU.run(MethPairWU.fss:11)

  - The same program with `extends Any` written dies alike under (i). So does `first[\U\](y: (U, U))` called as `b.first[\ZZ32\]((2, 3))`, which needs no tuple static argument.
  - Walk runs both: `one tuple parameter: 2`, `meth pair: 2 3`.
  - A plain method of a tuple-instantiated object (`same(y: T)`) and a top-level generic function at a pair run.
  - The one library's exposure looks small by a rough grep. Of 162 one-line, indented generic declarations in `Library/*.fsi`, none has a single parameter, besides `self`, whose type is a bare type variable or a tuple.
- **Under (i) only (rows 412, 470 and 691).**
  - The refusals in the table are row 412.
  - The written static arguments that pass are row 470: a top-level call's written static argument is not checked against its bound.
  - The drop of the pair's second element is row 691. The bound `Object` reaches it, and the bound `Any` does not (above).
- **The single-parameter overload rule.** `OverloadingChecker.checkBoundAny` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:469-472`, `:524-533`) refuses only an `extends Any` that is written, and so does walk (`interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:666-684`). An empty clause is exempt, as the specification says (F-174). Under (ii), `over[\T\](x: T)` beside `over(x: String)` is therefore valid and runs. This is no cost.

## How the compiled run time represents these types, and what ties them to `java.lang.Object`

- **`Any` on the JVM is the interface `fortress.AnyType$Any`** (`NamingCzar.java:138-140`). The following implement it:
  - every value class, through `FValue` (`compiler/runtimeValues/FValue.java:14`);
  - every tuple interface `AnyTuple⟦n⟧` (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:1676-1700`);
  - the erased arrow interfaces (`:990`).
- **A tuple at run time:**
  - the value is a `ConcreteTuple⟦…⟧` class, which extends `AnyConcreteTuple⟦n⟧` and implements `Tuple⟦…⟧`, below `AnyTuple⟦n⟧`;
  - `Tuple⟦…⟧` has typed getters `e1…eN`, and `AnyTuple⟦n⟧` has untyped `o1…oN` getters returning `java.lang.Object`;
  - its RTTI is `Tuple*n$RTTIc.factory(elements)`, which is covariant (`TupleRTTI.java:26-40`).
  - No tuple is a `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$Object`.
- **An arrow at run time:**
  - a closure extends `AbstractArrow⟦…⟧` and implements `Arrow⟦…⟧`, which extends the erased `Arrow⟦java|lang|Object,…⟧`, whose `apply` is `(Ljava/lang/Object;…)Ljava/lang/Object;`;
  - its RTTI is `Arrow*n$RTTIc.factory`, contravariant in the domain (`ArrowRTTI.java:41-57`).
  - An arrow class whose parameters contain `java/lang/Object` gets a `JavaRTTI(Object.class)` (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:1546-1552`; `runtimeSystem/InitializedStaticField.java:68-92`). Its `runtimeSupertypeOf` is always false (`compiler/runtimeValues/JavaRTTI.java:12`).
- **`()`** is `FVoid`, an `FValue` (`compiler/runtimeValues/FVoid.java`), with `VoidRTTI`. In class names it is `☃`, and in descriptors it is `Lcom/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FVoid;`.
- **`Bottom`** erases to `java/lang/Object` (`NamingCzar.java:1297-1306`).
- **The code generator ties an empty `extends` clause to `Object`.** `FnNameInfo.boundsFor` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/FnNameInfo.java:168-182`) erases such a parameter to the Fortress trait `Object` when it names a generic method (`NamingCzar.genericMethodName`, `:799-806`). Under (ii) the call reads `wrap☝✖Arrow⟦fortress|CompilerBuiltin%Object,…⟧`.
  - The name is only a name: the declaration and the call compute it the same way.
  - A written `extends Any` gives another name. An api and its users compiled under different settings would therefore still agree.
- **Java interoperability.** The native-wrapper mapping types a Java `java.lang.Object` as Fortress `Any` (`NamingCzar.java:447`), and `Lfortress/AnyType$Any;` as `Any` (`:333-336`). A native that is declared over `Object` or `Any` therefore already takes tuples, arrows and `()` by type. No run was made through a native with such a value.

## What the switch to `Any` would cost, in rungs (my reading)

- **One small rung for the switch itself.** It needs:
  - `Shell.java:372` set to `false` (walk already runs with it off, `Shell.java:380`);
  - the promotion of `XXXImplicitBoundAny` (row 412);
  - three pinned diagnostics rewritten;
  - the four `comprises` tests' `where [\E extends Object\]` written `where [\E\]`;
  - `XXXOverrideGenericReturnTypeNotSubtype`'s premise rewritten (row 653 surfaces);
  - `CoercionGenericFnCompiledRungC` given `T extends Object` until the switch-over, or left red until then.

  These touch 10 test files and no production code beyond the line. The 23 `CompilerSystem` tests need nothing.
- **No cost found for tuple or arrow static arguments in the shapes asked for.** They run under (ii) exactly as they run today with `extends Any` written.
- **Two run-time rungs that the bound does not cause, but that more programs reach once static parameters take tuples and `()`:**
  - row 339 (`()`);
  - the new tuple-domain defect of generic dotted methods.

  Each is one code-generator or class-loader rung. Neither shows in the compiled tracks.
- **The library's dispatch code changes in 6 classes**, deterministically, with no test showing it.

## What I could not measure

- **The one library on the compiled path.** The switch-over is not done. So its own instantiations at tuples, such as arrays indexed by `(ZZ32,ZZ32)`, did not run compiled; the shapes stand in.
- **The rest of the gate under (ii).** The misc track, `testSystem`, `testSpecData`, the ladder regression, the atomic runs and the demos were not run. By code reading, walk is unaffected: `useInterpreterLibraries` already turns the switch off.
- **The count stage.** F-289's 685 was not rerun.
- **Shapes left out:**
  - generic functional methods (with `self`) and inherited generic methods, at tuple arguments;
  - tuples of three or more elements, nested tuples, and arrows with tuple domains;
  - varargs and keywords, which the code generator refuses (`NamingCzar.java:1262-1265`);
  - a native receiving a tuple.
- **Thread counts.** The shapes ran at one thread only.

## Defects

1. New (codegen), compiled path only; walk runs it. A generic dotted method whose single parameter's type is a tuple, written or from a tuple static argument, dies at the call with `ClassCastException` in `castTo`. Reproducer: `object Box[\T\](x: T) first[\U\](y: (U, U)): U = do (a, c) = y; a end end` with `Box[\ZZ32\](1).first[\ZZ32\]((2, 3))`. Cause: `CodeGen.java:6250-6263` (above). This needs a new row in "12. The compiled path".
2. Row 339, confirmed by `javap`. The closure defines `apply(LFVoid;)`, and the interface `Arrow⟦☃,☃⟧` wants `apply()`. It occurs under both settings, and a dispatched generic arm reaches it too (`over(())`). The row's "unverified reading" can drop "unverified".
3. Row 691, reached by row 412: under the compile command as it is, `q = id((3, 4))` for `id[\T\](x: T)` compiles and runs `id(3)`, printing `q + 1 =  4`. This is a note for row 691 or row 412.
4. Row 470 is seen as `id[\(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]` and `id[\ZZ32 -> ZZ32\]`, which compile and run under the bound `Object`.

## Decisions

- **The patch form.** I made the patch a property defaulting to `true` rather than a hard `false`, so that the two settings ran on one build. The alternative was a hard `false`, with the old code run through `old-fortress.sh` for setting (i). With the variable unset, the code path is the compile command's own.
- **Setting (ii) includes the compiler's library compiled under (ii).** The alternative was programs under (ii) against a library analysed under (i). That would mix the bounds of the apis that the programs read.
- **Setting (i) of the 27 is taken from the gate.** The brief and the skill take the tree as passing. I ran it once more on the same build only as a control for the private caches folder, and it gave the same `OK (138 tests)`.
- No decision of the curator covers these choices.

## For FACTS

1. **The compiled path's run time handles tuple and arrow static arguments under the bound `Any`.**
   - The fact: with the pre-desugaring off, generic functions, objects, traits, dispatch to a generic arm and `typecase` at a pair or an arrow compile and run. They make the same classes and the same program bytecode as with `extends Any` written.
   - What it means: the switch to the bound `Any` costs the compiled path no run-time work for these shapes.
   - Shown by: the table above (command under "Commands"; no gated test).
   - Detail: "The shapes by setting" and "What the class loader makes".
2. **Under the bound `Any`, the compiled tracks give 12 failures in 10 tests of `CompilerJUTest`, and none in the library and othercompiler tracks. The 23 `CompilerSystem` `.test` files pass.**
   - What it means: the switch is one rung of test repair.
   - Numbers: 12 = 1 promotion, 3 pinned texts, 4 `comprises` workarounds, 1 premise (row 653), and 3 for one prelude limit (row 412's sibling, the prelude's `||` at `Object`).
   - Shown by: `FORTRESS_PROBE_BOUND_OBJECT=false ant testQuick` with the patch.
   - Detail: "The CompilerSystem tests, and the compiled tracks".
3. **`()` as a static argument fails at run time on the compiled path whatever the bound (row 339).** Detail: "What the code shows".

## Commands worked out

- **The setting switch.** The patch below, then `ant compileAll`. Then run the library order into a private folder with `FORTRESS_PROBE_BOUND_OBJECT=false FORTRESS_CACHES=<abs folder>`, the five `bin/fortress compile` lines of `build-and-caches.md`. `FORTRESS_CACHES` must be absolute: a relative one is read from `ProjectFortress/`, and the run then falls back to the bootstrap stubs with `NoSuchMethodError … coerce_ZZ32`.
- **The instantiated classes of a run.** `JAVA_FLAGS="… -Dfortress.bytecodes.expanded.directory=<dir>" bin/fortress run P` writes `<dir>/expanded.jar`, also when the run dies (`MainWrapper.java:66-71`). The entry names hold backslashes, so read them with Python's `zipfile` rather than `unzip`, writing each class to a plain file name for `javap -p -s -c`.
- **Both settings of the 27.** `FORTRESS_PROBE_BOUND_OBJECT=false FORTRESS_CACHES=<abs folder> ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh any ProjectFortress/compiler_tests <the 23 .test files>`, and the same without the variable, with the setting-(i) folder.

## Questions for the curator

- **When does the bound `Any` reach `fortress compile`?** Alternatives:
  - now, as its own rung, with the 10 test edits above;
  - at the switch-over, with the one library.

  Evidence: this report's track run. No decision covers it. P-42 says that the switch-over ends the departure, and F-289 says that the zero needs it.
- **What happens to `CoercionGenericFnCompiledRungC` if the bound changes before the switch-over?** Alternatives:
  - write `T extends Object` in the test;
  - make it an `XXX` test that names the prelude's `||`;
  - keep the bound `Object` until the switch-over.

## The probe-only patch (not landed)

# How the compiled-microGPT route was chosen — from the transcripts

Reconstructed 2026-09-20 from the raw session transcripts, not from the committed
documents (that reconstruction is `direction-history-documents.md` beside this file).
Sources: the archived coordinating session on the orphan branch `transcripts`,
`projects/-home-user-fortress/bdff267d-67dc-5bb9-b970-8c3dfaa634b6.jsonl.parts/{000,001}.jsonl`
(rejoined; one session, 2026-08-18 .. 2026-09-17T20:31:14Z), and the live coordinating
session `fe616d40-…jsonl` (2026-09-18 onward). Indexed with
`postmortem-2026-09-19/parse.py` over 2026-09-15T00:00Z .. 2026-09-19T06:38Z; indices
under `tmp/direction-history/` (gitignored). All times UTC. Quotations are verbatim from
`assistant-text.md` (what Pavol was told) and section A of `user-messages.md` (what he
typed); `[…]` marks an elision.

---

## 1. The exchanges

### 2026-09-15T10:06:06 — the option is put, without a recommendation

Coordinator, presenting the characterization inventory:

> **Five options for the next work, evidence for and against, no recommendation.** The
> compiled path for microGPT as a walking skeleton, which is the only option with a
> measured multiplier behind it and whose first two probes are named; […] The document
> says so under option 1 without recommending it. The ordering is yours.

No library question yet. The compiler's prelude is described only as a lack: the compiler
"lacks a 592-line prelude".

### 2026-09-15T10:42:06 — Pavol sets the goal in library terms

> I think fleshing out the standard library is one very important task to close it. […]
> I'd like to see that shape of the library extended so that the expression expressing the
> machine learning concepts with the matrices and tensors have the mathematical rigor that
> this flavor of library construction promises. […] what we first would need to do to get
> a performant stuff is not to box the doubles but have an array of doubles so that
> something usable can come out of this at runtime which the JVM compiler would be able to
> optimize so that goes straight onto the priority list

He says "the standard library", singular. Nothing in his message distinguishes the two
preludes, because at this point he has not been told there are two.

Coordinator, 10:45:07, answers about `Ring`/`Field` and the sealed tree, and adds:

> Making the checker usable on interpreter programs means giving it the interpreter's
> prelude, which falls under worklist item 2 and was never named on its own.

That is the library route, named once, in passing, as a checker matter.

### 2026-09-15T23:04:53 — the direction is first stated as an order, route (b) only

Coordinator, reporting the kernel benchmark:

> 1. **Nothing microGPT-shaped runs on the compiled path today.** […] The compiler's
> library has no `Array`, `Vector` or `Array3` types at all, not just no constructor.
>
> The order that follows, now on record in the knowledge base:
>
> 1. Give the compiler's library an `RR64` array type, so microGPT's kernels exist on the
> compiled path at all.
> 2. Fix the two one-line runtime defects […]
> 3. Unboxed doubles and `double[]` arrays, designed into step 1 rather than added after.

Pavol, in full:

> What's the compiler prelude that is so lacking?

Coordinator (2,277 chars), after describing `FortressLibrary.fss` at 4,518 lines and

> The two are separate worlds by design, not by accident […] A program written for one

Coordinator (01:19:33), step 5 of seven:

Pavol (01:25:21): *"You are still in the smart Alec register. Try again in plain English and

Coordinator (01:25:36), the plain-English restatement Pavol then acted on:

### 2026-09-17T01:31:22 / 01:43:51 / 01:51:55 — Pavol accepts the order

> And also, uh, later when you were talking about uh, building the numeric power, but we need

### 2026-09-17T17:15:25 → 17:44:11 — the next-climb analysis says the decision is not a name

**This is the moment the library route is reported as the thing the ladder is actually blocked
on.** Pavol's answer, 18:31:40, in the part that bears on it:

> I haven't read all your previous uh, responses […] So just hold very briefly this answer no
> no large just take it as a as a point to be answered next and I will try to go through your

And 18:51:26, after reading:

> Okay, I, I read all your responses. I don't know what to tell you now. Like, we need to fix
> what we broke. So, repair work needs to be done right fucking now. […] I am not sure how we
> selected the stuff for this first ladder climb. I, I recall vaguely that you said, like, we
> tried something and then counted the number of errors caused by a specific thing, and then we
> attacked them in order by how many things are fixed by this. Is this roughly correct? So. I
> understood that as something that must happen before we go to the array work. So it was just
> these eight things.

He redirects to the repair batch. **The question "more small rungs, or the sketch that decides
the array fork" is never answered**, and the library route is not mentioned again in the record
through 2026-09-19T06:38.

### 2026-09-18T00:00 .. 2026-09-19T06:38 — nothing

Nineteen typed messages in the live session in this window; all concern the lost container, the
transcript backup, worker pinning and the repair batch. No exchange touches the route. No
`AskUserQuestion` was ever used to put the library fork as a choice (the only two in the window
ask where the backup script should live and how much documentation churn to undo).

---

## 2. Summary

**Where the direction was fixed.** Twice, four hours apart on the night of 15–16 September,
and then once more on 17 September.

1. **2026-09-15T23:04:53** — "Give the compiler's library an `RR64` array type" enters the
   knowledge base as step 1, with no alternative named and nothing priced. Pavol had not yet
   been told that two libraries exist.
2. **2026-09-15T23:21:44** — asked what the prelude is, the coordinator names both routes for
   the first time and prices only route (a), by guess.
3. **2026-09-17T01:19:33 / 01:25:36** — "Choose route (b)", carried into the seven-step plan
   Pavol accepted at 01:51:55 with "Tag the tree and start with the concrete first step."

**What Pavol was told, and not told.**

- He was told there are two preludes, 4,518 lines against 592, and that the compiler's has no
  arrays and no algebra (09-15T23:21).
- He was told, as general architecture, that "every new execution path needs the whole library
  re-expressed in its world" and that the native layer "cannot be shared" (09-15T23:24) — but
  that sentence was aimed at the 2012 team, never at our own step 1.
- **He himself proposed the library route** (09-15T23:51: "Couldn't the path forward be just to
  use the FortressLibrary for compiler as well? What breaks and when?"), and the probe he
  provoked came back in its favour (09-16T00:13: 95% of the library is plain Fortress; "The
  natives are the small part").
- He was offered the fork twice, both times with "not needed yet" attached (09-16T17:43,
  17:49), and did not answer either time.
- He was **never** given a price for route (b). Not in lines, not in named types, not in months.
  The words "the library written twice" never appear; the nearest is the coordinator's own hedge
  "write it as the seed of one library, not a second one." Meanwhile route (a)'s price — "92
  checker errors and 108 native bindings" — was quoted at him twice as a reason not to take it,
  although the measurement that produced those numbers had been reported as *good* news a day
  earlier.
- He was told on 09-17T06:01 that the library route is a reserved fork that stops the climb —
  while the climb's ordinary work was already growing the compiler library toward it.
- He was told on 09-17T17:44 that the ladder is gated on the forks, not on names, and that the
  files behind `ImmutableArray` are really waiting on "the library route, your other reserved
  fork". He replied that he had not read it, then redirected to repairs. The question stands
  unanswered.

**So: was the compiler's own library chosen without pricing what re-implementing the arrays and
the algebra there means?** Yes. The one thing that was measured about either route was measured
about the route not taken, and it measured in that route's favour. Route (b) was chosen on the
argument that route (a) "is the right destination and the wrong first move", which is a
statement about order, not about cost — and no cost for (b) was ever put beside it.

**Earliest moment the record shows the coordinator knew the array slice would mean the library
written twice: 2026-09-15T23:21:44 UTC**, where it describes the choice as "either porting the
needed parts of the 4,518-line prelude into the 592-line one, or making the compiler consume the
interpreter's prelude" — the first option being, in plain terms, writing those parts a second
time. Three minutes later, at **23:24:29**, it states the principle outright: "every new
execution path needs the whole library re-expressed in its world […] it cannot be shared." Both
sentences are seventeen and twenty minutes *after* "give the compiler's library an `RR64` array
type" had already gone on record as step 1, and twenty-six hours before route (b) was formally
recommended.

content.content:
<!-- Judgement on which library the compiled world runs on and in what order the work goes, written 2026-09-20 on Pavol's permission by a delegated worker on the session's tier, from the evidence brief coordinator/two-libraries.md, POSITIONS.md (2026-09-16 on), reviews/array-design-review.md §3, FACTS.md, PLAN.md, the map, and the specification and source opened at the lines the brief cites. Read-only except this file; nothing was run. -->

# The library route: judgement

Terms. **Prelude**: the apis every program gets without importing them. **World**: a prelude plus its switches (`Shell.useCompilerLibraries()`); `fortress file.fss` runs the interpreter's world, `fortress compile` the compiler's. **Checker**: the static type checker, which runs only in the compiler's world. **Builtins**: the prelude's lowest layer, where declarations are bound to Java code (**natives**). **Exclusion**: the rule that two types share no value, which lets the checker refuse a trait extending both. **`nat`**: a static parameter that is a number, used for array sizes. **Rung**: one edit plus its test under the full gate (median 54 minutes). **Gated batch**: up to four rungs under one gate (3 to 5 hours landed). **Worker session**: one delegated report with its probe, no gate.

## 1. Is there a reason on record to keep a second library?

No. Nothing on record argues for two libraries as a destination, and Pavol's reading is the record's: the split was made on 2008-12-19 as a "stripped-down minimalist … first crack at compilation"; its switch is commented "hopefully temporary hack" in the tree today (`WellKnownNames.java:109-111`); the team called what went into it "bogus" (2009) and "bogo-trait" (June 2012, its last edit); the specification names one default library and never the compiler's (`library/structure.tex:13-22`, `default-libraries.tex:15-24`; no `.tex` in the tree contains the word `CompilerLibrary`). What the team did not leave is a plan for ending it: they grew the copy for three and a half years behind the wall they named at the wind-down, the type system against the JVM. That is a record of what they could do, not a position; overruling it costs nothing.

Each reason the brief and the reviews raise, judged:

- **A place the interpreter cannot see.** True (`next-climb/worlds.md`: an edit confined to the compiler prelude cannot reach the 384 interpreter tests) and never used: every batch gate has run `testSystem` anyway (`climb-batch-workflow.md:44`). Under one library a library edit is checked by both suites, which is the discipline Pavol set, not a loss. Not a reason for two.
- **Two native mechanisms.** Real, and a reason for two *binding* files, not two libraries: 95.3% of `FortressLibrary.fss` is plain Fortress; the natives are 108 bindings there and 231 in `FortressBuiltin.fss`, the builtins layer the specification itself separates from the library. Work before: re-bind those 339 (79 of the 108 have a `nativeHelpers` counterpart; the 231's overlap is uncounted, though the compiler's 330 `import java` aliases cover the same types). Whether the builtins are one text with `import java` on both paths, or one api with a component per path, is decided by a half-session probe nobody has run: `ForeignJava` is wired into the interpreter at `Driver.java:441` and exercised by no test. Not a reason for two.
- **The desugaring settings and the four well-known types.** One setting differs in substance: the compiler world gives an unbounded type parameter an implicit `extends Object`, and the specification says exactly that (`trait-parameters.tex:49-50`), so the compiler's setting is the spec's and the interpreter's is the divergence; the reconciliation keeps the compiler's. The four types (`String`, `JavaString`, `Exception`, `CheckedException`) are placed by `Types.useFortressLibraries()` once the world is one; the cost is the sources that name `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.X` literally (38 Java/Scala files, 21 of them the runtime's value classes such as `FZZ32`, plus the frozen stub `src/fortress/CompilerBuiltin.java`), a rename in the switch-over batch. Not a reason for two.
- **The checker's `nat` gap.** Blocks every route equally, growing the copy included, because the target vocabulary is sized (ruling of 2026-09-19). It is PLAN step 4 under any library. Not a reason for two.
- **The 27 exclusion sites.** The brief says only the `excludes` clause is in the specification. That is not right. The types chapter states three of the checker's four clauses: the `excludes` clause (`types-vals-vars.tex:212-214`), object-ness ("an object trait type excludes any type that is not its supertype", `:222-224`) and propagation to subtypes (`:163-164`). It does not state exclusion derived from `comprises`, and it contradicts the fourth clause: a trait "is allowed to extend other instantiations of itself" (`trait-parameters.tex:339-345`), while the checker's `checkP` (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:443-457`) makes two instantiations of one generic exclude each other, which is the shape of the numeric tower (`ZZ32 extends ZZ64`, both `Integral[\·\]`) and of the two reductions the library itself comments as a "Hack". Which clause fires at which of the 23 remaining sites was not traced. So this is work before: trace the clause per site (one worker session), then fix the library where a stated rule fires and the checker where the contradicted one does; a decision reaches Pavol only where the spec is silent, the `comprises` clause. The compiler world avoids this today only by keeping its tower flat (`ZZ32 extends { Number, Equality, StandardTotalOrder }`, no `ZZ64`, no `Integral`), the bogo-trait; a copy grown "in the library's own patterns" would meet the same rules. Not a reason for two.

One thing only one library gives: the checker on interpreter programs, which Pavol asked for on 2026-09-15 and which FACTS says means giving the checker the interpreter's prelude. It arrives the day the prelude passes TYPECHECK, before any native is ported.

## 2. The order

Destination: the compiler's prelude is the specification's, `AnyType`, `FortressBuiltin`, `FortressLibrary`, and `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra` are deleted at the switch-over. From `main` at the batch-2 landing:

**Step 0, now: stop adding to the compiler prelude.** Nothing is in flight (the tree is clean; the nine `wip/` remotes are landed batches awaiting deletion). The fourteen fork-free rungs were forecast to move 38 files by one phase and no microGPT component, and every one is a declaration `FortressLibrary` already has. Codegen rungs continue, being compiler work under any library: `forTryAtomicExpr` (row 353), `LetFn` (row 304), `ObjectExpr`, the eleven-file array-literal crash at `Misc.scala:876`. Prelude rungs (`Char`, `Thread`, `round`/`truncate`, `IndexOutOfBounds`) stop. The landed rungs' tests stay; the ten `library_tests` files that use compiler-world spellings (`NothingObject`, `Character`, `ZZ32Vector`) are rewritten at step 5.

**Step 1, the first rung: the interpreter prelude through the checker, as a gate stage.** Edit: `fortress typecheck` gets a `-fortress-lib` switch, the mirror of `-compiler-lib` (`Shell.java:860-863`; `typecheck` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` unconditionally today), or the 46-line `perf-probes/prelude/WorldFlip.java` moves into the harness; a stage in `climb-batch-workflow.js` beside the ladder regression runs the checker over the three apis and what they import under a private cache, prints the per-api error table and the crash line, and lands the table as the comparand. What it proves: that the distance to one library is measured by every gate from now on, and that the world switch is four lines. Stop condition: two runs print the same table (93 errors, 48 sites, 12 apis, `Not yet implemented` at `STypesUtil.scala:557`); the count is red, the suite is green; no library line changes. This is the one place the test-first rule is met by a stage rather than a `.fss`, because no program can yet be compiled against that prelude; the stage is permanent, which is what the rule protects.

Same batch, rungs 2 and 3, the defects with no question attached: family C, the fifteen `RangeInternals.fsi` bounds (`I extends AnyIntegral` where `Integral[\I\]` is required), 26 errors; families D and F and the site that extends and excludes `Condition[\()\]` in one line (`FortressLibrary.fsi:2526`), 4 errors. Gated by `testSystem`, which runs this code. Expected: 93 → 63 at 23 sites, nothing new. Stop: a fix that would change a declared type rather than a bound.

**Step 2, three worker sessions in parallel, no gate.** (a) The exclusion trace: for each of the 23 sites, which of the four clauses fires, beside the spec lines above; output: the sites under a stated rule (library rungs), the sites under the contradicted clause (a checker rung), and the sites under the `comprises` clause, the only decision that reaches Pavol. (b) The `nat` shadow session the review's decision F specifies: where the crash is (Scala or Java, finding 6), the export checker on the six dead-nat declarations (decision E: E2 in the checker, E3 the six-line api diff shown to Pavol), `NatExtends1`, `NatStore1`, and the loader probe that decides decision A (A2, the team's direction, against A3). (c) The half-session probe: a two-declaration component bound with `import java`, run by the interpreter; decides the builtins' shape for step 5.

**Step 3, the `nat` rung, then the exclusion rungs.** PLAN step 4 in the tree, shadow-proven, `.scala` plus whatever `.java` the shadow found: one to two gated batches. Decision E lands inside it. Then step 2(a)'s rungs, zero to two, or the `comprises` decision first. Stop condition of the phase: the stage prints zero errors and no crash, and `FlatArrays.fsi` type-checks with no error of its own (already true but for `nat`, FACTS). Milestone: `fortress typecheck -fortress-lib` works on interpreter programs.

**Step 4, one worker session: the prelude through DESUGAR and CODEGEN once.** No run has ever reached them with this library; the size is not on record. Output: the hole list, each hole a codegen rung, most of them rungs the ladder needs anyway.

**Step 5, the switch-over: at least two gated batches, with the one-`.java`-rung rule relaxed for them (as B1 proposed for the interpreter batch).** Batch one, the natives, re-bound as 2(c) decided: the 29 of 108 without a helper written, the 231 of `FortressBuiltin` matched to the compiler's helpers. Batch two, the names: the 38 sources and the frozen stub re-pointed; the two `useCompilerLibraries()` collapsed to one world with the extends-`Object` setting kept; the compile recipe's five files made three; the five prelude files deleted; the at least 48 compiler-side tests that name compiler-world spellings (a rough grep) rewritten to the spec's (`Nothing[\T\]`, `Char`). Gate: the full suite, the atomic runs, and the ladder regression, where the 85 passes must hold and the 104 fork-blocked files are expected to move off `Array is undefined`. Not settled: whether `FZZ32` implements `FortressLibrary.ZZ32` or `FortressBuiltin.Int` (the interpreter's `Int` is a value object under the trait; the compiler's value class is the trait's implementation); and, if 2(c) says two components, the mechanism, which is the step row 320 found missing (`Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`).

**Step 6, decision D: a diff, no code.** The model's static types (D1 with D3, the review's default) shown to Pavol as the diff of `rmsn` and `step`'s signature, as soon as step 3 lands and before any array rung.

**Step 7, the array rungs against the library's existing `Array`, `Vector`, `Matrix`, with no copy to write.** Decision A's `.java` rungs as 2(b) decided, at least three gated batches (finding 6: `IntArg` in `extends` at `CodeGen.java:5784`, a runtime kind for `nat` arguments, the store); then decision B, unboxing by static type in generated code (B2), the largest codegen work in the plan, its first measurement `kdot` compiled over the store against `KDotPrim`. End state: the 31 declarations of `FlatArrays.fsi` type-check and compile against the one library, the model's text as D decided.

## 3. Costs, and what each route forecloses

| step | units |
|---|---|
| 1 | 1 gated batch (3 rungs) |
| 2 | 2 worker sessions + 1 half session |
| 3 | 1–2 gated batches + 0–2 rungs, or 1 decision first |
| 4 | 1 worker session + codegen rungs, count unknown |
| 5 | ≥ 2 gated batches |
| 6 | one diff |
| 7 | ≥ 3 gated batches, then B, unmeasured |

To the point where the prelude is one and the checker passes it: about four to five gated batches and four worker sessions. The array work after it is the same under any route.

Growing the copy to the same target costs the copy itself, the array layer and the algebra above `Number` written a second time (about 1,200 lines plus `AdditiveGroup`, `MultiplicativeRing`, `Indexed`, `ReadableArray`, finding 3), at least three batches; plus the same `nat` rung, the same A and B, the same exclusion rules as its tower grows; and never the checker on interpreter programs. It is cheaper only for the 38 files it can move by one phase.

Forecloses. One library: the compiler world's spellings (`NothingObject`, `Character`, `Option`/`Some`), which the goal already rules against; the never-used sandbox; the 298 lines of revival prelude text, superseded, their tests kept. Two libraries: the checker on interpreter programs; the array vocabulary without a copy; the standard library ever being one thing.

Not settled by the evidence, in the order it is met: whether `import java` runs under the interpreter (2c); which clause fires at each tower site (2a); whether the `nat` crash is in Scala or Java (2b); whether the loader can select a representation (2b); what the library meets in DESUGAR and CODEGEN (4); the overlap of the 231 builtins with the compiler's helpers (5); the size of B (7).

## 4. The decision

What we do: make the specification's default library, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, the compiler's prelude, and delete `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra` when the switch-over lands; from now on no declaration goes into the compiler prelude, and codegen rungs continue.

What it changes: the standard library exists once; every library edit is gated by both suites; the checker becomes usable on interpreter programs when the prelude passes it; the array vocabulary is not written a second time; the thirteen revival commits to the compiler prelude are superseded and their tests kept.

Alternatives: keep growing the copy (reaches no microGPT component, runs out at 38 files, every line a copy to delete later); one text with two binding components for the builtins (a variant of the same destination, chosen by the step 2(c) probe, not by Pavol); both at once (two gates, no gain).

Default: one library, the interpreter's, with the builtins' shape decided by the probe. First rung: the interpreter prelude through the checker as a gate stage (step 1).

<!-- Why the compile path has its own standard library instead of the interpreter's, what the 2008-2012 team said about it, and what one library would cost by each of the three routes. Written 2026-09-20 by a delegated worker on Pavol's question. Evidence only: it costs the routes and recommends none. Every claim cites a file:line, a commit, or a run whose output is named. The one measurement taken live is a re-run of the prelude probe's driver under a private cache; nothing in the tree was modified except this file. -->

# Two libraries

Terms used below. **Prelude**: the set of apis the compiler implicitly imports into every component, so a program can name `ZZ32` without importing anything. **World**: a prelude plus the switches that go with it; `fortress <file>.fss` runs the interpreter's world, `fortress compile` the compiler's. **Rung**: one declaration added to a prelude with a failing test, gated on `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`.

## 1. When the split was made, and in whose words

The compiler's prelude was born on **2008-12-19** in commit `c8d301411` by **Jan-Willem Maessen** (`jmaessen`), whose whole message is: *"[libraries, interpreter] Preliminary version of stripped-down minimalist fortress library for first crack at compilation, plus interpreter support to let it all run through gracefully."* It created `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` (27 lines: two `print` bindings and an empty `trait String`), `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss` (49 lines), and the world switch itself, then in `interpreter/glue/WellKnownNames.java`.

The switch was documented as provisional in the same commit, in a comment that is still in the tree at `compiler/WellKnownNames.java:109-111`: *"Re-points fortressLibrary etc. to special compiler (rather than interpreter) versions of the code. **Hopefully temporary hack as we work on importing java objects cleanly.**"* Note the stated reason: importing Java objects. Not the type checker — the first `CompilerBuiltin` still bound its natives with `builtinPrimitive` and the interpreter's glue package; `import java` arrived three months later (`b2880c05c` 2009-03-03, *"We now import java.lang.Math, but we don't use it yet"*; `2f8744701` 2009-03-09).

Three further facts from the history. A **third** prelude existed for a month — `352c78880` (EricAllen, 2009-02-06) *"Added TypeCheckerLibrary and TypeCheckerBuiltin; threaded through front-end"*, removed by `904bd2684` (sukyoungryu, 2009-03-09) *"[type checker] Eliminated type checker libraries"*; its residue is `Types.useTypeCheckerLibraries()` (`compiler/Types.java:90-92`), which now just calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. The split's maintenance cost shows up early: `ce1366c17` (2010-02-25) *"Fixed a bug in Shell: use the interpreter library instead of the compiler library when running tests with the interpreter. (Found by Chulwoo Lee)"*. And the team had a word for what it was putting in the compiler's library: *"Tested by adding **bogus** Array traits in the CompilerLibrary. Tests should be added when generic traits can be compiled"* (`ccccbe26f`, 2009-10-04), *"It should use a parameterized Generator type but it is not yet supported. Instead, we use GeneratorZZ32 for now. Added **bogus** IN and = operators"* (`525264af1`, 2009-10-02), and, a month before the wind-down, David Chase's *"Added missing CMP method to **bogo-trait** ZZ32"* (`b16964470`, 2012-06-27). `compiler/Types.java:73-76` names the pair the way they thought of it: *"the compiler libraries"* against *"the full libraries"*.

**The specification knows one library, not two.** `Specification/library/structure.tex:13-22`: the automatically imported libraries are *"chiefly `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`"*; `library/default-libraries.tex:15-24`: *"Two sets of libraries are imported into every Fortress program by default"* — `FortressLibrary` and the builtins. `CompilerLibrary` appears in no `.tex` in the tree, and Sun's own `README.txt:432-437` says the same. The split is an implementation fact the published design never acknowledged.

**What no source says.** No commit message, no README, no text under `Papers/`, no spec `\note{}` states an intention to compile the full library one day, or any plan for ending the split. The record runs the other way: the compiler prelude was still being grown declaration by declaration in the project's last month. The wind-down note names the wall the project stopped at, and it is the same one — *"the mismatch between the (rather ambitious) Fortress type system and a virtual machine not designed to support it"* — while listing *"symmetric multiple inheritance with type exclusion"* among the eight things they were pleased with (`research/extracts/fortress-websites-wayback.md:110-123`). Exclusion is what two thirds of §3's errors are about.

## 2. What the two libraries share, and where they differ

**Sizes.** Compiler world: `CompilerLibrary.fss/.fsi` 718 + 358 lines, `CompilerBuiltin.fss/.fsi` 1,636 + 786 — 3,498 in all. Interpreter world: `FortressLibrary` 4,507 + 2,550, `FortressBuiltin` 701 + 218 — 7,976. `AnyType.fss` (17 lines) is shared. Since ladder rung 1 (`1bd8d3ad1`) the compiler prelude is four apis, not three: `compilerAlgebra()` is no longer commented out at `WellKnownNames.java:124`, which supersedes `map/dormant-code.md` §1.4. `Library/GeneratorLibrary` (469 + 314) remains unwired.

**Written twice.** Counting top-level declarations in the four api files by kind and name: 183 in the compiler world, 276 in the interpreter's, **75 in both** — 21 traits (`ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN64`, `RR64`, `ZZ`, `Number`, `String`, `Generator`, `Maybe`, `Range`, `Matrix`, `Comparison`, `TotalComparison`, `Reduction`, `Condition`, the exception roots), 27 objects, 9 operator names and 18 functions. The operator figure is by name and so under-reports: `opr` declaration lines alone number 346 in the compiler world's apis against 496 in the interpreter's. 108 declarations exist only in the compiler world, 63 of them the `characterXxx` category constants and the fixed-size integer bounds. **201 exist only in the interpreter's**: the array and range vocabulary (`Array`, `Array1..3`, `ImmutableArray`, `Vector`, `Indexed`, `Rank`, the `Range` family), the reductions and generators (`SumReduction`, `BigReduction`, `MonoidReduction`, `Comprehension`, `BigOperator`), the algebra above `Number` (`QQ`, `Integral`, `AnyIntegral`, `StandardTotalOrder`, `AdditiveGroup`, `MultiplicativeRing`, `LexicographicOrder`), `Thread`, and the factory and reflection functions (`array`, `matrix`, `vector`, `immutableArray`, `region`).

**The two native binding mechanisms.** The interpreter writes `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.Int$Less")` as the body; the evaluator pattern-matches that literal call and substitutes the named Java class for the body (`glue/NativeApp.java:157-215`, reached only from `interpreter/evaluator/values/FunctionClosure.java:47-57`), and the class takes the evaluator's boxed `FValue`/`FObject` and returns `FBool.make(…)`. 339 such bindings in the two interpreter prelude files (108 in `FortressLibrary.fss`, 231 in `FortressBuiltin.fss`), 427 across the whole interpreter library. The compiler writes `import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{simpleIntArith.intLT => jIntLT}` and then an ordinary call `jIntLT(self, other)`: 330 such aliases in 20 `import java` blocks, over 370 public static methods in 25 classes under `nativeHelpers/`.

**Could one text carry both?** Not in the `builtinPrimitive` direction: the name is declared only at `FortressBuiltin.fsi:30`, nothing under `compiler/` or `codegen/` refers to it, and a component that gives it a body compiles and then calls that body, the class-name string being inert data (`perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md` §3, `07-builtinprimitive-probe.out`). The other direction is **not obviously blocked, and this is new here**: `ForeignJava`, which reads a Java class with ASM and synthesizes an api for it, lives in the shared `repository/` package and is wired into the *interpreter* as well as the compiler — `interpreter/Driver.java:441`, `interpreter/env/ForeignComponentWrapper.java:59`, `interpreter/env/ClosureMaker.java:64`. None of the 381 `.fss` files in `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's own corpus, contains an `import java` line. So the mechanism is wired on both sides and exercised on one; whether an `import java` binding runs under the interpreter is one small probe that nobody has run.

**A difference that is not in the library files.** `Shell.useCompilerLibraries()` (`Shell.java:371-386`) flips three desugaring settings besides the prelude names, and one of them changes the language the text is written in: `setExtendsObjectPreDesugaring(true)` makes `PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.forStaticParam` (`:134-148`) rewrite an unbounded static parameter's extends clause in the compiler world and leave it alone in the interpreter's. `Types.useCompilerLibraries()` (`compiler/Types.java:72-83`) additionally re-points `String`, `JavaString`, `Exception` and `CheckedException` from the library api to the builtin one. A shared text has to be correct under both settings, or the settings have to be reconciled first.

## 3. The errors, classified

Re-measured for this brief rather than taken from the record: the probe's own driver (`perf-probes/prelude/WorldFlip.java` with its instrumented `StaticChecker` copy) re-run on the tree at `29a827877` under a private cache (`-Dfortress.caches`, honoured through `ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283`); `default_repository/` was not touched. Result: **93 errors at 96 locations across 48 declaration sites**, not the 92 on record. The extra one is the revival's own: commit `02d09a39f` (2026-09-19) gave `AnyIntegral` a `comprises { ZZ }` clause, and the checker now applies the comprises rule to `Integral[\I\] extends { …, AnyIntegral }` at `FortressLibrary.fsi:411`. Everything else is the same set shifted by three lines. The crash that follows is unchanged (`Not yet implemented`, `STypesUtil.scala:557`).

| family | errors | sites | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| A `Type X excludes Y but it extends Y` | 36 | — | see below |
| B `Types A and B exclude each other. C must not extend them` | 26 | 27 (A and B together) | see below |
| C `Ill-formed type` + `static argument I does not satisfy the bound Integral[\I\]` | 26 | 15 | library defect |
| D `multiple declarations of split / splitWithOffsets with the same parameter type: ()` | 2 | 2 (+2 secondary) | library defect |
| E `Invalid comprises clause: … should not be extended` | 2 | 2 | library against a rule the spec states only in a note |
| F return type not a subtype of the overridden one | 1 | 1 (+1 secondary) | library defect |

**A and B are one phenomenon under two message templates, and they are not one verdict.** The checker builds its exclusion relation from four clauses (`scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:423-457`): an explicit `excludes` clause (`checkEC`), a `comprises` clause (`checkCC`), object-ness (`checkO`), and **two distinct instantiations of the same generic ancestor** (`checkP`). Only the first is in the specification, which derives exclusion from `excludes` clauses and symmetry alone (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:218-228`). Of the 27 sites: **one** is a defect on anybody's reading — `FortressLibrary.fsi:2526` extends and excludes `Condition[\()\]` in the same declaration, which the spec's own *"neither can extend the other"* forbids; **two declarations across five lines** (`SumReduction` :1816-1818, `ProdReduction` :1827-1831) inherit one generic trait at two instantiations, with the library's own comment calling it *"Hack to permit any Number to work non-parametrically"*, a shape the spec neither permits nor forbids and about which it carries an open editorial question (*"Does it include instantiations of parametric traits?"*, `traits.tex:167-171`); the remaining **21** are the comparison, numeric and `Maybe` towers, where the checker enforces consequences of `comprises` that the spec states nowhere. Which of the four clauses fires at which site was not traced: the clauses were read, the per-site attribution was not.

**C is the clean case and it is a library defect.** `RangeInternals.fsi` declares four traits requiring `[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]` (`:44, :121, :235, :304`) and then instantiates them from declarations whose own parameter is unbounded (`object RightScalarRange[\I\]` at `:309`, `emptyScalarRange[\I\]()` at `:578`) or bounded only by the non-parametric `AnyIntegral` (`sized1Range[\I extends AnyIntegral\]` at `:580`, and nine more). The interpreter checks no static-parameter bound, so nothing ever reported them. D is the same kind of thing: `trait String` declares `splitWithOffsets()` and `split()` twice, once `abstract` at `:2311-2312` and once concrete at `:2327-2328`. F is a real covariance violation across two files: `List[\E\].zip` returns `Generator[\(E,F)\]` (`List.fsi:99`) where the `ZeroIndexed[\E\].zip` it overrides returns `ZeroIndexed[\(E,F)\]` (`FortressLibrary.fsi:1187`).

**The checker gap is not in this list.** It is the crash that follows it: `nat`, `int`, `bool`, `dim` and `unit` static parameters are unimplemented in the checker (`STypesUtil.scala:546-559`), and the interpreter's library carries 81 declarations that use them. That is a separate, already-planned step (`reviews/nat-checking-plan.md`, PLAN step 4) and it blocks routes (b) and (c) equally.

## 4. The three routes, costed

Units. A **rung** is one declaration plus its failing test under the full gate; the eight-rung climb of 2026-09-17 took 8h37m, median 54 minutes a rung (`iteration-cost.md` §A). A **gated batch** is up to four rungs under one gate, measured saving 58.2 minutes over eight (`batched-climb-plan.md` §9). A **worker session** is one delegated report with its probe, of which this is one.

**(a) Keep growing the compiler world's prelude — the standard library written twice.** Costed by what it has already done: eight rungs moved the compile-path pass count from 59 to 81 of 410 corpus files, +22 (`compile-ladder/CLIMB.md:44-50`), and thirteen revival commits grew the four compiler-prelude files by 298 lines. The next fourteen fork-free rungs are forecast to move 38 files, mostly by one phase and not to a pass (`next-climb.md` §0). *Blocks:* nothing; it is the only route that can proceed today without a decision. *Forecloses:* nothing technically, but 104 of the 303 non-passing `tests/` files sit behind the array representation, `nat` parameters or the generator tower, and none of those is reachable by a rung — so the route runs out before the target program, and every declaration it writes is the copy the other two routes would delete.

**(b) One library, the interpreter's, made to pass the checker.** Three pieces in this order (`perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md` §5). First `nat` kinds in the checker: PLAN step 4, five Scala/Java files plus an optional AST node, with a shadow-prototype recipe and a five-clause gate already written (`reviews/nat-checking-plan.md` §e, §f) — larger than a batch, smaller than a climb. Second the 93 errors at 48 sites: C, D and F (18 sites) are ordinary library edits, a batch or two; A, B and E (27 sites, the two E sites being among them) are not edits but a language-design conversation about `comprises` and exclusion, to be settled against the spec first — one worker session to state the question with the spec text and the four checker clauses beside it, then edits. Third the natives: about 79 of the 108 `builtinPrimitive` bindings in `FortressLibrary.fss` already have a `nativeHelpers/` counterpart under another name, about 29 do not, and the interpreter's remaining 319 bindings live in files the compiler world does not load. *Blocks:* every compiler-prelude rung written in the meantime becomes work to discard. *Forecloses:* the compiler world's own spellings where they differ — `NothingObject[\T\]`/`Nothing` against `Nothing[\T\]`, `Character` against `Char`, `Option`/`Some`/`NoneObject` against `Maybe`/`Just` (`array-design-review.md` §3c). *Does not settle:* whether the code generator can compile it. No run has ever reached DESUGAR or CODEGEN with this library.

**(c) One text, two native bindings.** The layer written once in `Library/`, with the native binding the only per-world file (`array-design-review.md` §3, decision C3, which records it as unprobed). *What is now known that was not:* the compiler's binding mechanism is wired on the interpreter's side too (§2), and no interpreter test exercises it, so the first experiment is one probe — a two-declaration component bound with `import java`, run under `fortress <file>.fss` — at roughly half a worker session. *What it still costs if that probe is green:* the same 93 errors and the same `nat` gap as (b), because a shared text meets the same checker; plus the three desugaring settings (`Shell.java:371-386`) reconciled and the four well-known types that the two worlds place in different apis (`Types.java:72-83`). *Forecloses:* the compiler world as a place to try a declaration the interpreter must not see — every rung of the last climb relied on exactly that (`next-climb/worlds.md`: an edit confined to `CompilerLibrary`/`CompilerBuiltin` cannot affect the 382 interpreter tests, with two named exceptions).

**Where the team's breadcrumbs point, and where they stop.** They point at the split being provisional, in their own words: *"hopefully temporary hack"* in a comment written the day it was made and still in the tree (`WellKnownNames.java:109-111`), *"stripped-down minimalist … for first crack at compilation"* in the birth commit (`c8d301411`), *"bogus"* in 2009 and *"bogo-trait"* in 2012 for what went into it, and a specification that recognizes one default library and never names the compiler's. They do **not** point at any of the three routes. Nothing on record says how the split was meant to end, or that it was meant to end at all; the last month of the project was spent adding to the compiler prelude. "Temporary" is evidence about intent, not about method: it is equally consistent with (b) and with (c), and it is not evidence against (a), which is what the team in fact did for three and a half years. The one thing the evidence does settle is negative and useful: the obstacle is not bytecode generation. 95.3% of `FortressLibrary.fss` is plain Fortress, and none of it has ever reached the desugarer or the code generator, because the checker stops it first.

---

## Appendix: the classification, site by site

Deduplicated and reported: 93. Compared against the captured `06b-typecheck-errors-only.txt` of 2026-09-16, the set is identical up to a three-line shift, plus one new error (family E at `:411`).

**Defects measured.** None is written to the ledger, because the brief keeps this worker out of the tree.

No row. Reproducer: `TupleParamOpr.fss` (section 3).
- **Static argument `Any` in an `extends` clause** stops the code generator. By my reading of `CodeGen.java:5786-5805`, `Bottom`, `Self` or an abbreviated type would stop it too. 2 declarations. No open row (row 411 is closed). Reproducer: `ExtendsAnyArg.fss`.

- **The refusals undercount the walls**, because a declaration is refused at its first wall. The parsed-tree site counts in section 3 bound the main constructs: 16 local-function groups against 9 refused declarations, 13 `asif` sites against 7, 8 `label`s against 3.
