content.content:
## 2. What the compiled world has

The compiler's own library is small: `CompilerBuiltin.fsi` 778 lines with a 1,627-line body, `CompilerLibrary.fsi` 356 with 718. It has no `Array`, `Array1`, `Vector` or `Matrix` with a body. The one `nat` declaration in it is `trait Matrix[\T, nat s0, nat s1\] extends Object end` (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi:279`), empty.

It has exactly one numeric array, and it is the shape the 2012 team chose for this world. `trait ZZ32Vector` (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:555-572`) has no static parameters at all: `shape`, `nrows`, `ncols`, `copy`, `opr[i]`, `opr[i,j]`, their `:=` forms, `|self|`, `fill`, `fill2`. Its body (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:1101-1136`) forwards every member to Java helpers imported at `.fss:299-305`. The Java class `FZZ32Vector` holds an unboxed `int[]` and four shape integers (`compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32Vector.java:18-19`); a 2-D index is folded to `(i-lower_x)*dim_y + (j-lower_y)` (`:65`); the whole class is 83 lines and its helper `nativeHelpers/simpleIntVector.java` 40. `NamingCzar` lists it as a special type whose implementation class is hand-written (`compiler/NamingCzar.java:553`, in the table declared at `:508-514`; also `:337-338` and `:461`). Above it, `CompilerLibrary.fss:484-535` declares `PREFIX_SUM`, `+`, `-`, `MIN`, `MAX` with a scalar, each a Fortress `for` loop over subscripts, and factories at `:587-593`. `StringVector` is the same design over `String[]` (`FStringVector.java:16`). Three live tests: `other_compiler_tests/VectorTest.fss`, `VectorTest2.fss`, `VectorTest3.fss`.

An element read on that unboxed vector still boxes. Verified in bytecode (§9, probe 2): `v[0]` compiles to a virtual call `FZZ32Vector."[]"(FZZ32) → FZZ32`, which calls `getValue`, which calls the generated native wrapper, which unwraps the index with `FZZ32.getValue()`, calls `simpleIntVector.getIndexedValue(FZZ32Vector, int) → int`, and re-wraps the result with `FZZ32.make(int)`; the caller then `checkcast`s. Four calls and one allocation per element. The storage is unboxed; the traffic is not.

The code generator lowers every type to a reference. `RR64` is `FRR64` (`NamingCzar.java:441-446` maps the bare JVM `double` to `RR64` only at the foreign-Java boundary); `x y` on two `RR64` is an interface call on `FRR64`, no `dmul` (`perf-probes/boxing/javap/CompilerBuiltin.juxtaposition_RR64.javap.txt:3559-3565`). The subscript node has no code-generation case of its own: `CodeGen.forSubscriptExpr` throws if reached (`codegen/CodeGen.java:4931`), so every `a[i]` is desugared into a method call on the array's trait before code generation.

Stamping renames; it cannot change a representation. Verified (§9, probe 1): the template for `object Box[\T\](x: T)` has the field `x` with descriptor `LT;`; the stamped `Box⟦FRR64⟧` has `Lcom/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FRR64;`. The substitution replaces one class name with another inside a reference descriptor. `[D` is not a class name, so no instantiation of a generic template can produce a `double[]` field, and the stamped interface's `get` returns the boxed class. The place the team left for anything cleverer is `if (false) { // Here will go all the magic expando-stuff. }` at `InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`.

The checker does not implement `nat` parameters, and the code generator carries them in names only; §6 has the full account. In one line each, verified (§9, probes 3-6): a nat passed explicitly to a function that uses it in no type compiles and runs; a nat that must be inferred from an argument is `Not yet implemented`; a nat-parameterised object instantiated with a literal crashes the checker with `ClassCastException: VarType cannot be cast to IntExpr`; a nat used as a value inside a function compiles to a reference to a class that does not exist and dies at run time. So sized array types cannot be declared on this path until the second fork lands, and unsized ones can be declared today.

The generic generator protocol exists here: `Generator[\E1\]` (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:614`) and `Reduction[\R\]` (`:638`). What is missing for arrays is `Indexed` and everything below it.

## 5. What the specification and the team's own drafts say

The specification's array is a family of sized types over a generic one, and it keeps both factories. The type of a k-dimensional array expression is `Array k[T, 0, n0, …, 0, n_{k-1}]`, abbreviated `T[n0, …]`, with a footnote that "As of March 2008, the Fortress library provides Array k types for 1 ≤ k ≤ 3" (`Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex:130-136`); a two-dimensional array of numbers "is a matrix", a one-dimensional one "is a vector", with the editors' margin notes reading "can be coerced to a matrix" (`:152-170`). The factory table gives `array[E](size)` for "the specified runtime-determined size" and `array1[E,n]()` for "statically determined size n" side by side (`advanced/parallelism-locality/arrays-distributed.tex:42-48`).

On storage: "As in Fortran, Fortress arrays are complex data structures; simple linear storage is encapsulated by the HeapSequence type, which is used in the implementation of arrays" (`arrays-distributed.tex:18-22`), with the note that distributions and `HeapSequence` "are not yet supported" (`:15-16`). Nothing in the prose says boxed or unboxed; the intent is an array as a structure over a linear store, which (c) is.

On sizes in types: "types can be parametric with respect to other types and values (most notably natural numbers)" (`preliminaries/intro/nutshell.tex:85-86`); the nat chapter is quoted in §6.

On the intended aggregate: "Guy's proposal for making tensors the principal user-level indexed aggregate type in Fortress (06/27/07)" and his email "Arrays, matrices, and tensors (short)" of 12/15/06 (`appendices/future.tex:63-65`); the FAQ's answer to variable-sized arrays with static bounds checking is a link to a wiki page that no longer exists (`appendices/FAQ.tex:55-57`); the emails themselves are not in the repository (`map/design-intent-sources.md:111, 128`).

On the compiled encoding: the JVM paper says "mentions of static parameters are replaced with their upper bounds in domain and range" (`Papers/Implementation/MethodMapping.tex:134`), which is why stamping is a renaming, and that the template's side file "contains info about the static parameters, including their names, whether they are types, oprs, or nats" (`:142`), which the tree does (§6). The team's own unboxing note is `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java:18-30`: four cases, "primitive. ZZ{8,16,32,64}, RR{32,64}, Boolean", singleton objects, unboxed fields, "comprises unboxed"; a taxonomy referenced by nothing.

The drafts say nothing about arrays. `Library/incomplete/` (24 files) contains no mention of an array. `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` and `.fsi` (783 lines, imported by nothing) are the generator and reduction protocol, `Container`, `DefaultGeneratorImplementation`, without `Indexed` or any array. `Fortress.Operators.fsi.INCOMPLETE` is the algebra above `Number` and names no aggregate. What the team shipped in this world is `ZZ32Vector`, and it is the only precedent with code behind it.

### 6d. The compiled representation of a nat-sized `double[]` array

Where the nat lives, two places, both needed: in the stamped class's name, `Vector⟦FRR64,16⟧` and `Vector⟦FRR64,4192⟧` being different classes, which the loader already produces from the mangled name (probe 6) and which is what makes the nat a fact for the checker and for dispatch; and as a run-time field of the native store (`dim_x` in the `FZZ32Vector` shape), because nothing today turns the name back into a value, the store's `get`, `put` and `|self|` need the number, and the `double[]` carries its own length. One class per distinct size is the price; microGPT's sizes are six literals and a computed 4192.

What the loader must do with a nat argument beyond what it does: supply a value for a nat in value position inside a template. Either the instantiater rewrites the `getstatic <Component>$n.ONLY` reference into a constant when it stamps `⟦…,5,…⟧` (an instruction-level substitution in `Instantiater`, the job the expando stub at `InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172` was left for), or the code generator emits a read from the run-time type descriptor, which today refuses `IntArg` (`CodeGen.java:5783`). Under the two-place representation the library's value uses of a nat are few (`i s1 + j` in `__DefaultArray2`, the `N[\s0\]` witness in `subarray`) and the store's field can serve the first; the second is explicit-only. So the value mechanism is a `.java` rung of its own, needed for the full port and not for the first kernels. Default: the field first, the name-to-constant substitution when the port reaches `subarray`.

Run-time sizes: `array[\RR64\](n)` with `n` computed cannot name its class at compile time. Either a native helper builds the stamped name from the integer and asks the loader for `Array1⟦FRR64,0,4192⟧` by that string, which is a string from a number and unprobed, or the run-time-sized factory returns the unsized `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` as it already does in the model (`FlatArrays.fss:14-17`) and only literal and symbol sizes get sized classes. Default: the second; it is what the model writes today, and the `reflect` group of §6c is then the one library pattern the compiled world does not reproduce until the first is probed.

174:- F-143 **Under walk, a type parameter whose bound mentions itself and that nothing at a call fixes is left open.** Such a bound is an F-bound, as in `mk[\T extends Cmp[\T\]\]()`. The open type, printed `OPEN`, is below every type, and every value matches it. A reduction or a comprehension that writes no static argument is first instantiated by its declared type or by its elements' join (F-228). So the open parameter reaches one only where neither fixes it: an empty `SUM` or `PROD` that no declared type directs, which takes `ZZ32`'s identity whatever its body's type (row 716), or a clause form whose declared type or join does not fit the bound (F-228). === 2026-09-23T07:16:28.611Z assistant (3685 chars)
Here is the whole thing in plain words, from the top.

**The problem.** A generic trait such as `List[X]` is a family of types. Suppose a library writes a generic function `tail[X](x: List[X]): List[X]` and, beside it, a faster special version `tail(x: List[ZZ])` for integer lists. Now suppose some object belongs to two members of the family at once, both `List[String]` and `List[ZZ]`. Call `tail` on it through a variable typed `List[String]`: the run-time dispatcher sees an integer list, picks the special version, and returns a `List[ZZ]` into a `List[String]` variable. The type system has been broken. So one of two things must be forbidden: the special version, or the double membership. Naden's write-up calls this "specialization of generic functions or multiple instantiation inheritance, but not both".

**What the type group chose, and what they weighed.** They kept the special versions and forbade the double membership. That is the rule in the checker. Naden's alternatives, each with its fate:

- Exempt some traits from the rule, chosen per trait. Measured by the probe: its other half refuses 69 pairs in the library, the tower's own method implementations. Out.
- Allow double membership when the type parameter is covariant. Does not rescue the tower, whose algebra traits use the parameter in argument positions. Out.
- Write generic functions with the self type as a bound, so the variable is tied to the value's own type. A style for library authors, not a checker rule, and Naden himself notes it fails behind an api.
- Filter at run time by the expected result type, or keep a separate overload set per call site. Rejected by Naden because programs become unreadable without static types.

He ends with "more work needs to be done". The conflict he names is our tower: `ZZ32` extends `ZZ64`, and each is an `Equality` of itself, so `ZZ32` is `Equality[ZZ32]` and `Equality[ZZ64]` at once.

**The commented-out code.** In the compiler's own small library, Steele commented out the extends clauses that would put the comparison traits onto the tower. So the compiled world's practical answer was: keep the rule, keep the special versions, flatten the tower, widen by coercion. That is the route "keep the rule". It contradicts the spec, which allows double membership, and your decision that the interpreter's library, with its nested tower, becomes the one library.

**The other trade.** The spec takes the opposite side of Naden's sentence: it allows double membership and forbids overloads of one name whose static parameters differ, which rules out the special version. It then fixes a generic's static arguments at the call site, so the call above uses `String` and the run-time value never chooses. The interpreter and the library grew up on this side. It is not on Naden's list because his group had chosen to keep the special versions.

**What the worker is sizing.** Only that second trade, because it is the one your decisions imply: what it costs to make the compiled dispatcher use the call site's static arguments, and what the spec's overload sentence refuses in the library and the test corpora. The last part is the real price: the library has about 35 places where a generic and a non-generic declaration share a name, and each family must become all-generic or merge.

**Your decision, when the note lands.** The type group's trade: rule kept, tower flattened, coercion added to the interpreter, special versions kept. Or the spec's trade: rule dropped, tower kept, dispatcher changed, about 35 library families rewritten, no special versions. 3:# The exclusion fork: a design brief for the route decision
5:## 1. The decision in plain words
17:## 2. The nine steps, compressed
19:### 2.1 The refresher
25:### 2.2 What each path does today, measured
33:### 2.3 What the specification says, dated
40:### 2.4 Where it sits in the tower
46:### 2.5 What the library already does
54:### 2.6 The peers, by family
62:### 2.7 The history, dated
71:### 2.8 The derivation from his principles
81:## 3. The three routes, priced from the notes
83:### Route A: keep the rule, flatten the tower
95:### Route B: drop the rule, instantiate at the call site, enforce the overload sentence
107:### Route C: the patents' forest rule
118:### Hybrids, and the counts that disagree
124:## 4. Weighing, as he asked
135:## 5. The recommendation
146:## 6. Open questions for him
- The forest for the tower plus the call-site fix, without the overload sentence, is route C as the forest note prices it: the sentence is not among its five pieces, and its overload half is the completion rule (`patents-forest-rule.md`, the routes). The notes hold no cheaper cut of C: dropping the return type rule leaves `ForestGeneric`'s hole open.
- A flat machine-width tower (`ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64` as coercing siblings, the specification's own example) with ℤ inside ℚ inside ℝ kept as subtyping would still need the forest rule for the upper chain, since `ZZ` carries `Equality` at `ZZ`, `QQ` and `Number`; its price is A's conversion sites for the fixed widths only plus all of C. No note splits the survey's sites by level, so this hybrid is named here, not priced.
- The counts disagree by tree and by instrument. 93 to 33 (`REPORT.md`) was rung P's relaxation on the pre-L base `d610695c0`; 103 to 24 (`patents-forest-rule.md § 4`) is the same switch on today's tree after rung L's api repairs; 103 to 22 (`price-keep-the-rule.md § 5`) is the flat library under the stock checker, and its two fewer are the `comprises` errors the flat `AnyIntegral` makes well formed; 103 to 37 is the forest. All four are the gate's instrument, which stops the `FortressLibrary` api at its hierarchy stage. The scope note's 203 (`scope-call-site-dispatch.md § 5`) is the zero probe's stack, which repairs that stop so the overloading check reaches the api; it is a deeper instrument, so its 203 to 382 under the sentence cannot be laid beside 22, 24 or 37.

## 4. Weighing, as he asked

- The premise (`POSITIONS.md:80`): the specification "was written in a vacuum early on", "as a wish"; the type group "knew much more about what's feasible"; "when that wish met reality, then the spec must change"; strong weight on "whatever Naden was thinking and where he was driving the design".
- Applied to the dated facts, the premise selects: the rule stays, because it is the group's implemented and published position (2010-2011, Steele among the authors, restated in 2012 and 2019); the overload sentence carries no weight, because it is 2009 text never revised and enforced by neither path; and `Empty extends List[\T\]` and ℤ-inside-ℚ-as-subtyping carry little, because the compiled checker never implemented them. That puts route B outside the premise: its footing is the spec sentence and the interpreter.
- Between A and C the premise's own facts split. For A: the compiler prelude's flattening is the group's implemented resolution of this exact conflict in the compiled world (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen, 2009-2010), and their last published line (POPL 2019) has no self types and no tower. For C: the patents are the latest thing they wrote (2012-08-31, after the flattening, Naden and Steele among the inventors) and they keep the tower; but they are claims, never built, their self-typed dispatch step is commented out in Welterweight, and the checker's one comprises-based attempt overflowed (2012-06-06).
- Where the facts complicate the premise: the interpreter and its library are the group's too, and they kept the nesting and refused the shortcut to the end; the sentence B rests on was never enforced, but neither was the nesting ever checked by the compiled checker; and "where Naden was driving" points two ways on one day, the self-type bound `add[\X <: Ring[X]\]` (a flat tower's idiom) in his write-up and the forest in the patent.
- What the premise does not settle: it ranks texts by date and by whether they were implemented, and the two implemented halves are both the group's, their reconciliation implemented by no one. So between A and C the premise leaves a judgement, not a ranking, and the judgement below is made on what is measured against what is derived.
- The case for A, as its advocate would put it: every peer he named flattened, the team's own compiler prelude flattened, the specification's own mechanism between widths is coercion, every number is measured, and no type theory of ours goes into the checker; the count falls furthest; the interpreter gets the mechanism the team left a TODO for; and microGPT's text changes nowhere under remedy (i).
- The case for B: the specification and the interpreter, both theirs, allow the type and refuse the shortcut, and no gated interpreter program uses the shortcut; every static-resolution peer allows the double membership; the code is 22, 43 and 19 lines, all measured, with the prelude and 43 generic tests unchanged; the tower and row 330 stay as decided; the 179-pair repair is padding both paths already accept.
- The case for C: it alone keeps all three things the group built, the rule, the nested tower and the shortcut; it is their last word; the checker half is built and lifts 48 of 61; the completion is seven declarations and the rule 40-70 lines; the markers it cannot lift are read nowhere; the library's shape, the specification's ℤ inside ℚ and row 330 change not at all.

## 5. The recommendation

Route A, keep the rule and flatten the tower, with the interpreter taught coercion (remedy i) rather than the sites converted by hand. The reasoning: it is the one route in which nothing is derived, every number comes from a survey over the whole test corpus, and the checker, the part he has said he cannot judge, is not touched; it is the group's own implemented resolution of this conflict (the compiler prelude, 2009-2010) and the shape of every high-performance peer he named; under his premise the two things it gives up, ℤ inside ℚ as subtyping and `Empty extends List[\T\]`, are early spec text the compiled checker never implemented; and the shortcut, which the group's late work was built to keep, stays. B is not chosen because its footing is the weakest text and, as measured, it either keeps the tower's inner-level hole or refuses the tower's own methods. C is not chosen because its soundness rule is ours, not theirs, and building it is the type-theory design he has said he does not want to own.

- Cost in the project's units: two rungs, each gated on the full suite (a gate run is 739 s, `microgpt-run-c-handover.md:16`). By batch 3's rate, 1.64 M tokens and about 80 minutes per rung landed (`coordinator/climb-batch-3-cost.md:19`), so about 3.3 M as a two-rung batch; the batch 3.5 estimate for two rungs is 7 to 13 agents and 2 to 4 M (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-3.5.md:191`). The library rung is the larger.
- What he would be committing to: the library's tower takes the prelude's shape for good; ℤ inside ℚ inside ℝ becomes three coercions and a recorded spec deviation; the interpreter chooses coercions at run time, a recorded divergence from the specification's static rule; `Empty extends List[\T\]` stays unsupported on the compiled path; `SUM` and `PROD` are redesigned; the `AnyIntegral` closure's `NOT YET` comment and its five-line accommodation of 2026-09-21 are withdrawn as moot; row 330's rationale is restated on coercion with its decision unchanged; the tripwire test is deleted.
- What stays open and comes back to him: which of the three `SUM`/`PROD` replacements; generic inference over mixed widths (`lo:hi`); the interpreter outputs that change when a wide binding really widens; and the two code-generator defects and the overloading checker's blindness to symbolic operators, which are holes under every route and not in the ledger yet (`dispatch-and-route-c.md § 3`).
- What a no to every route costs: the switch-over stays where rung P left it, 61 of the 103 errors at the tower, the tripwire test standing, no library batch that touches the numbers briefable, and the checker-count stage holding its 103 (`REPORT.md`, "The stop"; `POSITIONS.md:77`).
- The first rung to build: the interpreter coercion rung. It calls the already-lifted `coerce_<trait>` functions at `OverloadedFunction.bestMatch` ("TODO add checks for COERCE"), at the single-closure sites and at the typed bindings, about 150-200 lines in six files, with the keep note's `FlatCall`, `FlatOverload` and `FlatBind` probes as the tests written red first, and no library line changed. Today's nested tower needs no coercion, so the gate stays green on it, and it is the prerequisite the library rung cannot do without (`price-keep-the-rule.md § 3, § 6`).
- If he chooses B, the first rung is the 43-line call-site fix for top-level functions with `MieDispatchSub` and `ScopeArms` as its gated tests, since it is measured, changes no gated output, and B and C both need it (`scope-call-site-dispatch.md § 3`). If he chooses C, the first rung is the measured `checkP` change with `comprises T` on the seven traits and the markers dropped, count declared 24, with the return type rule probed in a shadow before the second rung is briefed (`patents-forest-rule.md § 4`).

## 6. Open questions for him

- Is ℤ inside ℚ inside ℝ64 as subtyping, the reasoning of row 330, something the language must state itself, or is coercion between them acceptable as the specification already has it between machine widths (a yes to subtyping points to C, not A)?
- Does he weigh the patents' forest rule, the group's latest text but never built, above the compiler prelude's implemented flattening of 2009-2010 (a yes points to C)?
- Does the judge's reading of "one library, the interpreter's" as forbidding the prelude's tower shape stand, or did the decision settle only which files survive (if it stands, A is out)?
- Is the specialisation shortcut something the one library must keep, or would he give it up, which is what B needs and what, under the wider reading of the sentence, ends in a flattened tower anyway?
- Does he accept the interpreter choosing coercions at run time, a recorded divergence from the specification's static rule, or must the interpreter match the compiled path's static choice, which turns A's first rung into the by-hand conversion of 367 sites?

The item 35 probe is back. Its data confirms form 1, and one small choice remains for you.

**What the probe found**
- **Form 1's compiler half works and costs 1 rung.** The rewrite is 116 lines plus 4. It compiled and ran correctly all five cases: a plain function, a trait's method, an object's method, an overflow error, and two helpers sharing one name. 17 existing compiler test files still pass.

- **Form 2's checker half is quiet.** 20 of `ZZ32`'s natives converted to `import java` were all accepted, and the distance stayed at 105. A deliberately wrong binding was refused, so the check is real.
- **One gap in form 1:** a misspelt helper string would slip through and fail only when run. The rung needs a rule that refuses a string naming no helper.

**The choice:** when does the checker start seeing the natives under form 1?
1. **Rung by rung, from the first natives rung.** Each rung's bindings are checked as they land. A bad binding shows up in the rung that wrote it. This needs a stand-in table of type names from that first rung on; the switch-over needs that table anyway.
2. **All at once, at the switch-over.** Nothing is checked before then. About 350 bindings meet the checker on one day.
3. **Form 2 instead.** The same checking as option 1, but every body changes to the compiler library's form, which the specification doesn't have.

**What a yes to 1 means:** the natives work starts with the loader rung for the interpreter and the rewrite, test first. Then come about two batches of library strings, alongside the checker batches.

goal of the runtime is to choose the most specific applicable definition so that as much information can

On the other hand, when we consider the runtime system, we realize that there is a strong

Ultimately, Fortress implements blanket multiple instantiation exclusion for the semantic

team's own `ProjectFortress/tests/conditionalExtension.fss` the same way from its

**One premise of the brief, corrected by the history.** The compiler prelude was not
flattened by Guy Steele in 2011. David Chase cut the subtyping on 2009-08-31 ("ZZ32 is NOT
a subtype of ZZ64, RR32 is NOT a subtype of RR64; this would be a good time to get
coercion working", 6896886fb); Sukyoung Ryu added the exclusions (3e0306166, 2009-10-16);
Jan-Willem Maessen with Eric Allen, Justin Hilburn and Scott Kilpatrick made ZZ32 coerce
IntLiteral "as described in the spec ... as we gradually migrate to a flat numeric
hierarchy" (128f313b5, 2009-11-17); Eric Allen added ZZ64's coercions from IntLiteral and
ZZ32 and RR64's from RR32 and FloatLiteral (2ef730c88, d0cde7d17, 2010-01); Steele then
built on the flat prelude: the ZZ32 and ZZ64 operators (da5291587, 2011-07-22), the ZZ32
big + and big MAX (d535963cb, 2011-10-12), and ZZ's coercions from all four fixed widths
(304f2743a, 2012-06-12).


### 7. The history in the commits

2008-07-15 (fca589bbb): IntLiteral under ZZ32 "and thus under every other numeric type";
"all the ZZ32 math you do will end up yielding results of type Int", and too-large
literals evaluate to a ZZ. 2009-08-21 (116e5e6fa): "ZZ32 and RR64 arithmetic can't be
commingled at all at the moment" in the compiler. 2009-08-31 (6896886fb): the compiler
prelude flattened. 2009-11-17 (128f313b5): IntLiteral coercion "as described in the spec",
toward "a flat numeric hierarchy". 2010-01-06 and -13 (2ef730c88, d0cde7d17): ZZ64 and RR64

# The three specification artefacts: what each one is, and how they relate

## Summary

- `Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf` is the real 1.0 release artefact: added
  2008-03-31 by the team (`403afbe0b`). The LaTeX **sources** sitting next to it in
  `Specification-1.0-frozen/` are not 1.0 text — they are a January 2012 clone of the
  then-current working draft, made by Guy Steele, and they are still today the working
  draft in 202 of 208 tracked files.
- `Specification/` is that same working draft, carried forward. The team's last edit to
  its text is 2010-12-09. Nobody touched it again until the revival built and committed
  a rendered PDF from it in 2026, under the label "July 19, 2012" — a date the revival
  chose, not the team, and not the date of any edit.
- `Documentation/Specification/` is a separate, later, unfinished restart: begun
  2012-02-20 by Victor Luchangco, restructured and substantially written by Steele and
  Luchangco through May 2012, abandoned on 2012-05-31 with a 65-page draft PDF and most
  chapters still empty skeletons. Two of its finished chapters (Types, and part of
  Lexical Structure) are, by date, newer team prose than anything in `Specification/`.

content.content:
## 2. Why Steele froze the draft in January 2012

`c02fa44d0` ("Cloned Specification directory into Specification-1.0-frozen", Guy Steele,
2012-01-04) sits inside a week of intense work by David Chase and Jean-Baptiste Tristan
on operator static parameters and RTTI (`b24a48a3c`, `4305f45d9`, `5d1c1b5ce`,
`30b00ab60`, all 2012-01-04 to 01-13) — none of it touching the specification. Nothing in
the surrounding commit messages states a reason for the clone.

What the record does show is what happened *after*: the team never again edited
`Specification/`'s text (confirmed by the date-order tree walk below); instead, five and
a half weeks later, Victor Luchangco started a **different, new** directory,
`Documentation/Specification/` (`166841592`, 2012-02-20), and by May 2012 Steele had
joined him in restructuring and writing it (§3). Read against that sequence, the January
clone reads as Steele setting the existing draft aside — freezing it as a fixed
reference point — just before the team began rethinking the specification from scratch
rather than continuing to edit the old one. This is a reading of the sequence, not a
stated reason; no design note, README, or mailing-list text in the tree says so in words.
(`explorations/reviews/spec-change-form.md:237-239` reaches the same reading
independently: "Before a large revision (2012). Steele copied the whole directory ... and,
four months later, began a new document instead of editing the old one.")

The name "1.0-frozen" is misleading taken literally. `git diff --quiet
2f8b4331a:Specification c02fa44d0:Specification-1.0-frozen` succeeds (verified directly)
— the clone is byte-for-byte the working draft as it stood on 2011-02-02, not the 1.0
text. Today the two source trees still differ in only 5 of 208 tracked files: the
revival's restyling of `fortress/fortress.tex` and its three `fortress/*.pl` table
generators (`4672b71cd`), and one historical stray `\tracingcommands=1\tracingmacros=1`
line at `Specification/basic-lib/objects.tex:17` that is absent from the frozen copy
(`explorations/coordinator/map/spec-to-implementation.md:109-111,117`). The only
genuinely-1.0 content near it is the PDF beside it (§1).

## 6. The consequence: which artefact is the team's latest statement, topic by topic

The project's goal names `Specification/` — "the July 2012 draft" — as the standard to
finish the language against. On the great majority of the language, this is simply
correct: `Specification/` is not only the largest and most complete of the three (596–599
pages against 262 for the 1.0 PDF and 65 for `Documentation/Specification/`'s last
build), it is also, on every topic `Documentation/Specification/` never got past a
12-to-30-line skeleton for, the team's only and therefore latest statement. That covers
static parameters (`trait-parameters.tex` — the exact chapter behind the multiple-
instantiation-exclusion question that prompted the batch-4 specification rung has **no**
corresponding file at all in `Documentation/Specification/Prose/`, skeleton or
otherwise), traits and objects beyond a stub, exceptions, components and APIs, the memory
model, parallelism, dimensions and units, and the entire numeric-tower library part.

On two topics, though, `Documentation/Specification/` genuinely holds later team prose
(§3): **Types**, where `types.tick` (Victor Luchangco, 2012-05-31) is a complete,
from-scratch rewrite dated a year and a half after `Specification/`'s last edit to the
matching chapter; and, more partially, **Lexical Structure**, where a newer but
admittedly incomplete chapter exists alongside the older, fuller one. On these two
topics, if "the team's latest statement of the language" is read literally, it is the
unfinished `Documentation/Specification/` text, not `Specification/` — though that text
was never finished, never checked against the rest of the language definition, and never
adopted as the specification of record before the project ended. This is offered as
evidence bearing on Pavol's decision of what to cite where; it does not by itself say
which text should govern.

# Dating five spec sentences against the type group's 2010-2012 implementation work

Method: `git log --all -- <path>` (no `--follow` — it drags in unrelated
commits here; `--all --follow` returned 152 commits for a file with one real
edit, because rename-detection latches onto content in the ~146 parentless
full-tree snapshots this conversion created). Every path below shows only
5-6 such snapshots reachable from `--all` (2011-12-06 to 2012-07-19), each a
byte-identical re-add of the same blob — spurious "touched" credits, not
revisions (`explorations/repo-internals.md:90-96`). The real incremental
edits, where any exist, sit only in the severed pre-2011 island reachable
from `0f49d8698` (2009-11-06, Sukyoung Ryu, "Added the entire spec files").
Dating is by direct blob diff between that commit and HEAD (`a874948ac`).

**Caution on `Specification-1.0-frozen/`**: for `basic/overloading.tex`,
`basic/trait-parameters.tex` and `advanced/overloading.tex`, the file there
is byte-identical to the final 2012 HEAD copy (including HEAD's 2010
copyright bump on `advanced/overloading.tex`) — not an independent 2008
snapshot for these three, whatever its name claims. Only
`basic/types-vals-vars.tex` differs there from HEAD (missing later,
unrelated additions), so only for that one file does frozen corroborate.

**1. `types-vals-vars.tex`, the subtype/exclusion "smallest ones" paragraph
(:147-227).** Byte-identical between `0f49d8698` (2009-11-06, Sukyoung Ryu)
and HEAD (2012-08-31) — confirmed by direct diff, not just presence — and
present at the same lines in the (here genuine) frozen copy. Never revised
after 2010, or after 2009. No clause about "instantiations of one generic"
was ever added: the file's only match for "instantiation" is an unrelated
sentence on type aliases (line 606) — the multiple-instantiation-exclusion
rule was never written into this section.

**2. `trait-parameters.tex:339-351,365-367,383-397`** ("extend other
instantiations of themselves", the `C extends D[\T\]` and `Empty extends
List[\T\]` examples). Byte-identical `0f49d8698` (2009-11-06, Sukyoung Ryu)
to HEAD. The file's only diff across that whole span is a copyright reword
(Sun→Oracle) and one unrelated note added elsewhere. Never revised after 2010.
result: byte-identical `0f49d8698` (2009-11-06, Sukyoung Ryu) to HEAD,
never revised.

**5.** Four of the five are 2008/2009 text the git record shows untouched
straight through the type group's 2010-2012 implementation push: the
exclusion-relation "smallest ones" paragraph (item 1), both
`trait-parameters.tex` passages (items 2 and 4), and — decisively for the
question this was asked to settle — the `overloading.tex` (basic) sentence
that static parameters must not differ and "do not enter into the
determination of which declarations are applicable" (item 3). That sentence
was last touched, per git, by Sukyoung Ryu no later than 2009-11-06, a year
before the multiple-instantiation-exclusion rule entered the checker
(2010-05-28), and it was never revised afterward: it is early thinking, not
a post-hoc rationalization of the checker rule. The one passage that
genuinely moved in this window is the *advanced* overloading chapter's Meet
Rule preamble, not item 3's sentence — rewritten and copyright-dated to
2010 by whoever did it, but git cannot name who: that commit is one of the
~146 severed links, absent from `--follow`, path-scoped `-S`, and an
unrestricted repo-wide `-S` alike.

=== 2026-10-24T11:41:16.444Z assistant (6016 chars)
I'm holding batch 23, as you asked. The worker that updates the "Revival So Far" page is running. Your questions in order, then the steps I propose.

## Can we trust the zero?

**As a measurement, yes.** The distance stage runs the compiled checker over the library's 12 core apis and their 12 components. It runs every check of each, whatever an earlier check found. No error is filtered or counted out by hand.

**But it's "zero errors the checker can see".** Four things limit what it sees:
- **Scope.** The 12 components are 12 of the library's 53. microGPT also imports `System`, `File`, `FileSupport` and `FortressAst`. A check of those four this morning found 31 errors (24 in `FileSupport`).
- **The checker's own blind spots.** The three readings, below, and other known holes in the gap ledger where the checker accepts too much. For example, at a top-level call it doesn't check a written static argument against its bound (row 470).
- **Library edits made to satisfy the checker.** Most use the team's own devices: a written static argument, `cast`, an `excludes` clause. Some removed api promises the component never built; batch 22 dropped six subscripts and four getters. Some are readings of ours. Nobody has yet sorted them all against the designers' intent.
- **Code generation.** The checker says nothing about it. The code generator refuses 50 declarations the checker passes (F-34).

So your instinct is right: the zero is real, but there's debt beside it that nobody has tallied.

## Your restatement of the three readings

- **Row 816, `abstract` api members:** you have it right. Under the other reading the distance is 1 until 12 lines are written. This morning's probe also showed that, as landed, 9 library calls would die at run time once compiled.
- **Row 731, unwritten reduction arguments:** this one isn't a skipped count. The checker can't work out the element type of `BIG MIN[i <- r] f(i)` unless the type is written, as `BIG MIN[\ZZ32\][i <- r] f(i)`. Your decision P-78 says to write it, and the library now does. So the library's zero is honest. A user program that leaves the type out is still refused.
- **Row 782, top-level symbolic operators:** right. The export check doesn't compare `+` and its kin between an api and its component. When a probe turned that on, it reported 165 entries. Those look like a fault in the check itself: it reports names spelled alike as missing. So the true number there is unknown until the check is fixed.

## Natives

Your understanding is correct. Walk's library bodies name Java classes by strings. We move each to a static helper in `nativeHelpers/`, which both walk and the compiled path call. Of the 449 bindings:
- 154 already have a compiled helper with the same signature, so only the string changes;
- 59 have a helper under another name;
- 158 need a new helper, written from walk's Java body;
- 78 wait, for example `NativeArray`, `Thread` and the I/O objects.

## The two questions, more simply

- **Q1, the distance stage in phase 4's gates.**
  - The gate is the full check before a batch lands: the build, the test suites, and two stages that run the checker over the library. It isn't about test coverage.
  - Once a binding moves to a helper, the checker compares the binding's declared types with the helper's Java types. The count stage reads only the `FortressLibrary` component. The distance stage reads all 12.
  - Your decision P-39 runs the slower distance stage only in batches meant to lower it. Ke

### Minor 11. What the specification's own breadcrumb on unboxed arrays says, which the design does not cite

Jan's note #82 on unboxed types (`appendices/future.tex:42`): "Do we want to permit arrays of fixed bounds to be unboxed? No. Unboxed arrays are a different other thing. Among other things, an array of fixed bounds may be a segment of another array." That is the team saying that a sized array is a structure (possibly a view) over a linear store and that the store is the thing to unbox, which is the shape of option (c) and of `HeapSequence` (`arrays-distributed.tex:18-22`). It supports the design's separation of sized traits from a native store; it should be in §5.

### Minor 12. Two numbers in §3 are the review's, not the tree's

### Decision A. What puts `double[]` under the library's sized traits

What we do: choose the mechanism by which `Vector[\RR64,16\]` gets a `double[]` store while `Vector[\T,16\]` for other `T` gets a boxed one.

What it changes: which `.java` rung the array work needs first, and whether the library's generic factories keep their text.

Alternatives. (A1) The design's default, a factory selecting by run-time type tag under one generic storing object: refused by the checker (finding 2); to keep it, a code-generator special case for the factory, a `.java` rung with no team precedent. (A2) The team's direction: the code generator and loader give a stamped `PrimitiveArray⟦FRR64,n⟧` a `double[]` field, `Unbox.java` case 1 plus the expando stub; the library's text stays as it is; the largest change, in the loader and `CodeGen`, and `PLAN.md` step 5's own first probe. (A3) Monomorphic storing objects per native element type (`__RR64Vector[\nat s0\]`) beside the generic boxed one, with a monomorphic factory name per element type in the manner of `array1`/`vector` (`.fss:2251`); typed cleanly, no code-generator change, but the model then names `rr64vector`, not `vector`, and the generic `Vector[\T,s0\]` is boxed for every `T` including `RR64` unless the user calls the right factory.

Default: probe A2 first (one shadow experiment, `next-climb.md` §3b's first item), because it is the team's breadcrumb and `PLAN.md`'s order; A3 is the fallback that needs no `.java`; A1 is closed by the probe unless Pavol wants the special case.

### Decision B. Where loops run unboxed

What we do: choose between Java natives per whole-array operation and unboxing `RR64` by static type in generated code.

What it changes: whether the ruling "it cannot be boxed" holds for the model (views, lambdas, `rows`) or only for whole-array operations on stores; and the size of the code-generator work.

Alternatives. (B1) Natives first, the design's default: measured at 8.9×/6.6× primitive on the model's shapes (finding 4), the same as boxed storage; helps `p DOT p` and Adam only; no precedent. (B3) Both, in the order B2 for element access and arithmetic, natives only where a whole-array kernel beats the JIT (a measured residue, not a default).

Default: B2, because it is the only alternative under which the ruling is true of the model, and the kernel measurement in the array rung is then `kdot` in Fortress against `KDotPrim`, not against a native.

125:Because instantiated generic types can only extend other ground types, and can only mention ground types as static parameters, the set is closed.  The transitive closure of the extends lists (not the subtype relation, but the lists themselves) cannot mention the same generic stem with different parameters more than once, so the number of types generated for each instantiation is proportional to the size of the closure of extends lists; this is judged to be an acceptable cost. Covariant generics with Any-bounded static parameters (for example,  \ftt{AnyList[\BS\ T extends Any \BS]} will create special headaches because Tuple and Arrow type relationions are far too large to encode into the Java type system.  One possibility will simply be to forbid that case; otherwise, it can be implemented by wrapping values, and using a method to implement strict equality, not just a pointer comparison.

# Is boxing the ceiling on the compiled path? A measurement

The record says the bytecode compiler lowers `RR64` to the runtime class
`FRR64` and emits no `DADD` (`explorations/repo-internals.md:129`), and that
compiled microGPT-shaped code runs 6.8-8.9x faster than the walk interpreter
(`explorations/compiled-path-gaps.md` §1b). From those two facts it is natural
to infer that *boxing is the ceiling* and that unboxed doubles and `double[]`
are the first thing performance needs. This probe turns the inference into a
measurement: the same loop in the interpreter, in compiled Fortress, and in
Java over boxed objects and over primitive `double`, all on one host with one
JDK, plus the generated bytecode that settles what "boxed" means here.

**Short answer: the inference is half right and the ordering is wrong.**
The compiled loop is 156x slower than the same loop over primitive `double` in
Java. Boxing — a fresh heap object per arithmetic result, allocation and
indirection included, measured with escape analysis defeated — accounts for
**2% of that gap**. The other 98% is three things the generated code does per
iteration that have nothing to do with the representation of a number: it
re-derives each float literal by formatting a `double` to a decimal string and
parsing it back, it guards every read and write of the loop's accumulator with
a transaction check whose debug message is built eagerly, and it runs the
"sequential" `for` loop as a recursive binary subdivision over boxed indices.

What this set keeps of the designers': the exclusion rule and the flat tower; the team's `Vector` and `Matrix` as additive groups; the self type read from the bound, as Naden asked; the three overloading rules and existential reduction with bounds, as POPL 2019 has them; `comprises` on values with the team's own `where` spelling closing its hole; conditional extension where the team's two texts needed reconciling; the `Index` bound the team wanted, with the one rule they could not write marked as the revival's. What it still departs from, knowingly and recorded: the tuple rule; P-60's static uniqueness; coercion between widths in place of nesting; `ZZ32` ranges; `IntLiteral` for the Working Draft's numeral types.

## 5. POPL 2019: where the chain follows the paper, where it goes outside its proof, and which is a risk

**Follows the paper.** P-42 (the default bound `Any`, p. 11:9), P-45 and P-152 (Fig. 5, Fig. 6 and existential reduction), P-48 (the intersection of the upper bounds, never `Bottom`, pp. 11:19, 11:25), P-43's rule ([Anc-Same-Trait]), P-62's road ([D-Method]). Each confirmed in the recheck and unchanged since.

**Outside the paper's proof, a silence.** Functional methods, top-level functions, closed types and nominal exclusion are omitted and said to be addable "in an obvious way" (extract §1, §6); coercion, `nat` parameters, tuples and numbers are absent. P-146's body-half intersection is outside FGFV's syntax, inside the static checker only. P-156's tuple rule is outside the paper (no tuples) and against the Types chapter, a designers' text, not the paper. These are silences: the paper neither supports nor refuses them.

**Outside the paper's proof, a stated restriction, and so a bounded risk.** (a) F-bounded method parameters, the library's `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and every function over `T extends Integral[\T\]` (F-271): the restriction "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" protects the paper's one-pass right-to-left solve at run-time dispatch (p. 11:11). Where the parameter is fixed by an invariant argument position, `Generator[\T\]`, the bound is checked and never solved, so microGPT's reductions carry no risk; a generic reached only by dispatch with an F-bounded parameter not fixed by an argument would, in phase 5. (b) P-60's run-time uniqueness against Theorem 4.1: a stated theorem given up at calls between closed traits; its cost is code generation on intersection results (rows 540, 559) and it is recorded (`changes.tex:3521-3525`). (c) P-146's signature half avoided a third: Lemma 5.2's hypothesis that a declared type holds no type parameter inside an intersection (`ParkPOPL2019.txt:1098-1107`). The hypothesis is about matching ilks against declared types at dispatch, in phase 5; a self-typed trait's `X` is also fixed by its invariant receiver instance and by `other: X`, so matching has the parameter from other positions; the risk is real only for a dispatcher built as the paper's, which the compiled path does not yet have (row 538). Change 1 of section 4 touches none of this: the static exclusion test is not matching.

**Where he is "very wary to go against" the paper**: nothing in section 4's changes goes against a rule of the paper. Change 1(ii) is the paper's own reduction. Change 1(i) uses a fact the paper has no words for (self types) in a static test it does not model. The paper is silent on self types, on tuples as indices, on coercion and on the library; it does not decide P-156 or P-157 either way.

=== 2026-09-16T00:13:03.265Z assistant (2288 chars)
You were right to push on it. The answer, measured (`explorations/perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md`):

**Almost nothing in the library is specific to bytecode generation.** 211 of its 4,518 lines are the 108 native bindings; the other 95% is plain Fortress. And most of the natives already have compiler-side counterparts under other names (355 static methods in `nativeHelpers/`, covering about 79 of the 108).

**What breaks when you use `FortressLibrary` as the compiler's prelude, in order:**

1. Fed to `fortress compile` as it is: 1,417 errors. All of them are name collisions because both preludes are in scope at once. An artifact, not a real failure.
2. With `FortressLibrary` made the prelude (the worker did this through a driver, no tracked file touched): name resolution passes with zero errors.
3. The type checker then reports 92 real errors in the library's own numeric and comparison hierarchy: traits that exclude each other and also extend each other, `Integral` bound violations, one bad `comprises`.
4. Then the checker crashes: `Not yet implemented`. The Scala type checker does not support `nat` static parameters at all. A six-line program with one `nat` parameter fails on the compile path and runs on the interpreter. The library has 81 such declarations; C4's vocabulary has 30; the compiler's own prelude has one, the empty `Matrix`.
5. Desugaring and code generation were never reached, so no bytecode-specific failure has been seen yet.

So my guess was wrong in its shape. The library does not "fail the checker in places nobody counted"; it fails in 92 counted places, and then the checker itself gives out on the sized types. The road is: implement `nat` parameters in the checker first, fix the 92 tower errors second, port the natives third. The natives are the small part.

Two more things this settles. Your dimension-checking question from yesterday: the static check that `nat` types promise is not implemented anywhere, not in the interpreter (checker off) and not in the compiler (checker crashes on them). And the compiled path's missing array types are the same wall seen from the other side: they were left out because the checker could not have checked them.

Recorded in `FACTS.md`, superseding my guess, and in the handover. Nothing is running.

You have it right, and I can put the finger on it.

**What the 92 errors are.** Yes, that was the earlier probe: feed the interpreter's library to the compile path and see. Name resolution passes. Then the type checker, which only the compile path runs, reports 92 errors in the library's own numeric tower, things like a trait that both extends and excludes another, and then crashes because it does not implement `nat` and the other static-parameter kinds at all. So the interpreter's library has never been type-checked, and when it is, its tower is inconsistent in 92 places.

**Why the split exists, as far as the record goes.** The interpreter came first, with its natives as glue classes over boxed values and no checker. The compiler came later, with natives as plain static Java methods, and the team wrote it a small prelude that does pass the checker, growing it as they went. Whether they meant that prelude as a bootstrap toward compiling the full library one day, or as a permanent second library, is not on record yet. That is the part a worker has to dig out of the history.

**What the ladder climb was doing.** Not unifying. Every rung added a name to the compiler's prelude, which is the "written twice" route by default. The reviewer's finding is that the array design silently continues it with one line, "into the compiler's prelude". Your instinct, one library, is the reserved fork the plan named and nobody has opened.

**Action taken.** An Opus worker is now writing the evidence brief: the history of the split in the team's own words, what the two libraries share and where they differ, each of the 92 errors classified as a library defect, a checker gap, or a real disagreement with the specification, and the three routes costed in rungs and batches. Judgement comes after, with your permission if you want it at Fable level.

Recorded as your leans, to confirm: for the unboxed store, the team's own direction, the class loader, unless a clear reason appears; for the library, one library, not two.

In one sentence: nothing on record argues for keeping the compiler's second library. Every reason raised is work to be done before one library can serve both worlds, not a reason for two. The team's three and a half years of growing the copy is a record of what they could do behind the JVM wall, not a position to overrule.

**The decision, for you.** What we do: the interpreter's library becomes the compiler's prelude and the compiler's three prelude files are deleted; no new declaration goes into the compiler's prelude from now on; code-generator rungs continue. What it changes: the ladder's fork-free library rungs stop, the array layer is built once against the library's existing types, and the checker becomes usable on interpreter programs on the way. **The first rung:** run the interpreter's library through the checker as a gate stage, so the distance to the goal is measured at every gate. It changes no library line. Its stop condition is two identical runs.

**Cost:** about four to five gated batches plus four worker sessions to a checked prelude, then the switch-over, then the array rungs. The copy route would build the array layer twice and never give the checker on interpreter programs.

content.content:
=== 2026-09-08T19:39:54.049Z assistant (2113 chars)
The written record agrees with your reading, and it says where the performance mandate went.

**The money left in 2006.** Fortress was Sun's entry in DARPA's High Productivity Computing Systems program. When DARPA chose the Phase III vendors in late 2006 it kept Cray and IBM and dropped Sun. From then on Fortress was a Sun Labs research project on a research budget, and the work that followed was the specification, the type system, and the interpreter. The compiler to JVM bytecode only started around 2008.

**What they said stopped them.** Steele's July 2012 wrap-up post, which we hold as an extract at `research/extracts/fortress-websites-wayback.md`, does not blame arithmetic speed. It says they hit "severe technical challenges having to do with the mismatch between the (rather ambitious) Fortress type system and a virtual machine not designed to support it (that would be every currently available VM, not just JVM)." The runtime class generation for generics was their attempt at that mismatch, and it is written up in the papers under `Papers/RuntimeInstantiation` in the original tree. So the boxing and the unspecialized generics were not an oversight they planned to fix later. They were the frontier they were still fighting when the project ended.

**Was there a plan for an optimizing compiler?** Not as a document I can point to. The bet, stated in the early design papers, was that a JVM target would inherit HotSpot's optimization for free and that the language's implicit parallelism would deliver the speed at scale. Both halves depend on the semantic overhead being compiled away, and they never got to that stage. The code generator does contain some unboxing and specialization code, which I have only seen by name and not read.

Your verdict stands on the evidence: expressivity and the parallel model were the research, and performance was deferred to a runtime that could not carry it.

If you want the recorded plans collected properly, a scout through `Papers/`, the spec's implementation notes, and the 2008 to 2012 commit messages is one Opus worker. Not launching it unasked.

# The nine tenets of the revival: their grounds, by layer

Evidence worker's map, read-only, tree at `24314b0b9` (branch `main`), 2026-10-26. I ran nothing that edits the tree. I give no verdicts.

**The curator's frame.** His message of 2026-10-26T05:25:27.242Z (T-now): "I hope you are incorrectly mixing the aspects: what Fortress does with how is Fortress implemented on JVM and probably related is a topic of interoperability with Java." His goal behind the switch-over, 2026-10-26T04:47:50.485Z (T-now), as the brief cleans it: "The whole point of the switch-over is to avoid the need to port walk's library into the compiler's library. The revival is continuing the development of the type checker, so that it would accept the fuller Fortress library that the interpreter uses."

**The three layers.**

- **L1, the language**: the Working Draft, the revised specification, the papers, the 2012 restart, the team's library as a statement of the language, and the team's later published word in `research/extracts/`.
- **L2, the team's implementation on the JVM**: the compiled path's checker, code generator, class loader and run time, and what the team's code and commits show it needs. Walk is also an implementation; I file it under L2 and name it.
- **L3, Java interoperability**: how Fortress types and natives meet Java types and classes.
- **"L2→L1"** marks a ground of one layer used as the reason for a choice in another layer. The first layer named is the ground's, the second the choice's.

**Abbreviations.**

- POS = `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`; HIST = `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS-history.md`; FACTS = `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`; "row N" = gap-ledger row N; "rq N" = item N of `explorations/coordinator/review-queue.md`.

POS.md:7:

The revival revises the specification to reconcile contradictions: where the team's later work, in the compiler or in the papers on types, contradicts the original text, the text is updated to follow that work (P-26: the type group's later word wins). The language is not redesigned. The specification is a living document that states each change that the revival makes (P-95 says how a change is recorded). ## Tenet 3. One library, the interpreter's (P-37)

> - P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. ## Tenet 7. Unboxed doubles and `double[]` arrays (P-17, P-84), on the compiled path's template classes

### (a) The entries

POS.md:16:

> - P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.

POS.md:92:

> - P-84 **An `RR64` array is stored as a Java `double[]`, unboxed, and arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, the library's own practice is the standard). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). The compiled path's `double[]` store waits with the other array decisions until after the switch-over; among them is decision A, how an `RR64` array made through the library's generic array traits gets that store (P-85).

## Tenet 9. Walk runs the checker after the switch-over (P-12, with P-59)

### (a) The entries

POS.md:12:

> - P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).

POS.md:56:

> - P-59 **Walk chooses a coercion by the run-time value until it runs the checker, after the switch-over.** Walk has no static types. So where a coercion is needed, walk chooses it by the value's run-time type. The specification and the compiled path choose it by the static type. The curator accepts this as the interpreter's limit, and walk is not changed for it before the switch-over. A callout in the coercion chapter (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex`) states the limit. ## Tenet 3. One library, the interpreter's (P-37)

### (a) The entry

POS.md:34:

> - P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled). The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library may take a design of the prelude's, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library. The decision is not put to him again. How the checker comes to accept the library, its first step and the order of the work, was left to a plan for him, which he approved (P-33).

Linked: P-38 (POS.md:35), P-33 (POS.md:30); pointed to by F-11 (FACTS.md:9).

## Tenet 7. Unboxed doubles and `double[]` arrays (P-17, P-84), on the compiled path's template classes

### (a) The entries

POS.md:16:

> - P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.

POS.md:92:

> - P-84 **An `RR64` array is stored as a Java `double[]`, unboxed, and arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, the library's own practice is the standard). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). The compiled path's `double[]` store waits with the other array decisions until after the switch-over; among them is decision A, how an `RR64` array made through the library's generic array traits gets that store (P-85).

> - P-58 **Every native binding is a `builtinPrimitive` call naming a static helper.** A native binding is a library body that is exactly `builtinPrimitive("…")`, the library's own form, and it keeps that form. ## Tenet 9. Walk runs the checker after the switch-over (P-12, with P-59)

### (a) The entries

POS.md:12:

> - P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).

POS.md:56:

> - P-59 **Walk chooses a coercion by the run-time value until it runs the checker, after the switch-over.** Walk has no static types. So where a coercion is needed, walk chooses it by the value's run-time type. The specification and the compiled path choose it by the static type. The curator accepts this as the interpreter's limit, and walk is not changed for it before the switch-over. A callout in the coercion chapter (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex`) states the limit. Two expected-failure tests record it: `XXXCoercionStaticRungC`, the chapter's own printed example, and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC`. After the switch-over, once walk runs the checker on its programs (P-12 orders the two steps), it uses the static coercions that the checker inserts. MicroGPT's static types are concrete, each the type of the value itself and not a trait above it, so on microGPT walk's choice and the static choice agree.

Linked: F-9 (FACTS.md:8), F-128 (FACTS.md:159).
